domain.title: Architecture & Performance
domain.tag: CPU · memory hierarchy · GPU · profiling · mechanical sympathy
domain.why: This is where you find out computers aren't as fast and uniform as they seem — some ways of writing the exact same logic run ten times faster than others, purely because of how the hardware moves data around. Most programmers never learn this and just accept whatever speed they get. The ones who do learn it can make things fast on purpose instead of by luck, and it's one of the most visible skills a systems engineer can have.

L0.body:
# Unpipelined: one instruction occupies the whole datapath for 5 units.
#   throughput = 1 / 5 instructions per unit time
#
# Pipelined into 5 stages, 1 unit of work each, plus 0.1 latch delay:
#   cycle time      = 1 + 0.1 = 1.1
#   steady throughput = 1 / 1.1
#   speedup         = 5 / 1.1 = 4.55x   (not 5x)
#   latency per instruction = 5 x 1.1 = 5.5   (WORSE than 5)

concepts.L1: Split one long combinational datapath into $k$ stages separated by latches. Each stage handles a different instruction in the same cycle, so the machine retires one instruction per cycle instead of one per $k$ cycles. Cycle time falls to roughly $T/k$.
concepts.L2: Pipelining makes no single instruction faster. It makes them faster per unit time. Per-instruction latency actually rises, because every stage boundary adds latch setup and clock skew that the unpipelined datapath never paid.
concepts.L3: Let the unpipelined path take $T$ and split it into $k$ balanced stages with latch overhead $\ell$ per boundary. Cycle time is $T/k + \ell$, so throughput speedup is $T/(T/k + \ell)$, which approaches $T/\ell$ and not infinity as $k$ grows. Latency becomes $k(T/k + \ell) = T + k\ell$: strictly worse. Two further costs bite as $k$ grows. Stages are never balanced, so the cycle is set by the slowest one. And a control misprediction discards everything in flight, a penalty proportional to depth. The Pentium 4 pushed to 20 and then 31 stages chasing clock frequency and lost to shorter, wider designs.

L4.prompt_tpl: An unpipelined datapath takes {T} ns per instruction. You split it into {k} balanced stages with a latch overhead of {l} ns per stage boundary. Give the steady-state throughput speedup and the new per-instruction latency. Answer with the throughput speedup.
L4.answer: speedup $= T/(T/k + \ell)$; latency $= T + k\ell$. For $T=10, k=5, \ell=0.2$: cycle $=2.2$ ns, speedup $=10/2.2=4.55$, latency $=11$ ns.
L4.explanation: Throughput is one instruction per cycle time, and cycle time is the stage work plus the latch. Latency is $k$ cycles. Notice the two answers move in opposite directions: this is the whole trade, and it is why deep pipelines are a throughput decision, never a latency one.

L4.prompt_tpl: As the stage count $k$ grows without bound with latch overhead $\ell$ fixed, what does the speedup {expr} converge to, and what physical cost grows linearly in $k$?
L4.answer: It converges to $T/\ell$: once the latch dominates the cycle, adding stages buys nothing. The cost growing linearly in $k$ is the branch misprediction penalty, since a flush discards every stage in flight.
L4.explanation: This is the quantitative reason the industry stopped chasing depth around 2004. Frequency scaling ran into the latch floor at the same time as it ran into the power wall, and the misprediction penalty was rising the whole way.

L0.body:
IF   instruction fetch      -- read memory at PC, PC += 4
ID   instruction decode     -- decode, read register file, sign-extend
EX   execute                -- ALU op, or compute effective address, or test branch
MEM  memory access          -- data cache read/write; nothing for ALU ops
WB   write back             -- write the result into the register file

# lw  r8, 0(r9)     uses IF ID EX MEM WB   (result ready end of MEM)
# add r10, r8, r11  uses IF ID EX --- WB   (result ready end of EX)
L0.cloze:
The five stages are {{c1::IF}}, {{c2::ID}}, {{c3::EX}}, {{c4::MEM}}, {{c5::WB}}.
A load's result is ready at the end of {{c6::MEM}}; an ALU result at the end of {{c7::EX}}.

concepts.L1: The teaching pipeline: fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back. A RISC instruction set is designed so every instruction fits the same five slots, which is exactly why loads and stores are separate instructions rather than addressing modes on arithmetic.
concepts.L2: This is not a historical toy. It is the shape every later mechanism is a patch on: forwarding patches EX-to-EX, the load-use stall patches MEM-to-EX, and out-of-order execution is what you build when you refuse to stall. Learn its stage boundaries or the rest is memorisation.
concepts.L3: The order is forced. You cannot read registers before you know which registers, so ID follows IF. You cannot address memory before computing the address, so MEM follows EX. You cannot write the register file before you have the value, so WB is last. Now count where values become available: an ALU result exists at the end of EX, a load's value only at the end of MEM. That one-stage gap is the load-use hazard, and it is the reason MIPS originally exposed a delay slot after loads. CISC hides this by cracking `add eax,[mem]` into micro-ops that occupy the same slots, so the five-stage model still explains an x86 core's dependence timing even though no x86 core has five stages.

L4.prompt_tpl: In the five-stage pipeline, why must {stage_a} come before {stage_b}? Answer in terms of what data is not yet known.
L4.answer: ID before EX: the ALU needs operand values and an opcode, and neither is known until the instruction word has been decoded and the register file read. EX before MEM: the data address is computed by the ALU from base plus displacement, so there is no address to send to the cache until EX finishes.
L4.explanation: Each boundary exists because the next stage needs a value the previous stage produces. This dependency chain, not tradition, sets the stage order, and it is what makes the load-use gap unavoidable.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {k}-stage pipeline runs {n} instructions with no stalls. How many cycles from the first fetch to the last write-back, and what is the steady-state CPI? Answer with the number of cycles.
L4.answer: cycles $= n + k - 1$; CPI $= (n + k - 1)/n$, which tends to 1. For $k=5, n=1000$: 1004 cycles, CPI $= 1.004$.
L4.explanation: The $k-1$ term is the fill. It is negligible for long runs, which is why pipeline depth is invisible in throughput benchmarks and very visible in anything that flushes often. Every flush pays the fill again.

L0.body:
# DATA hazards, by the order of the accesses
add r1, r2, r3      # writes r1
sub r4, r1, r5      # RAW  (true dependence)  -- real, must be respected

add r1, r2, r3      # writes r1
add r2, r6, r7      # WAR  (anti-dependence)  -- naming only

add r1, r2, r3      # writes r1
add r1, r6, r7      # WAW  (output dependence) -- naming only

# STRUCTURAL: two instructions want the same port in the same cycle
# CONTROL:    the next PC is not known until the branch resolves
L0.cloze:
{{c1::RAW}} is a true dependence and cannot be removed by any hardware trick.
{{c2::WAR}} and {{c3::WAW}} are naming hazards, removed entirely by {{c4::register renaming}}.

concepts.L1: Three reasons a pipeline cannot simply advance every cycle: two instructions need the same hardware resource (structural), one needs a value another has not produced (data), or the machine does not yet know which instruction is next (control).
concepts.L2: Only RAW is a real dependence. WAR and WAW are artefacts of having a finite number of architectural register names, and renaming deletes them completely. Engineers who treat all three as equally fundamental cannot explain why out-of-order execution works at all.
concepts.L3: Take the RAW pair `add r1,r2,r3` then `sub r4,r1,r5`. Information must flow from the first to the second; no amount of hardware invents the value early. Now the WAR pair: the second instruction writes `r2` while the first still needs to read it. Give the second write a fresh physical register and the collision evaporates. Same for WAW: two writes to `r1` only conflict because a later reader must see the right one, which renaming resolves by construction. So the taxonomy predicts the machine: renaming is a complete answer to two of the three, forwarding and scheduling attack the third, and structural hazards are answered by duplicating ports.

L4.prompt_tpl: Classify each dependence in this sequence and say which ones survive register renaming: (1) `mul r{a}, r2, r3` (2) `add r5, r{a}, r6` (3) `sub r{a}, r7, r8`.
L4.answer: 1 to 2 is RAW (true) and survives renaming: instruction 2 genuinely needs the product. 2 to 3 is WAR and 1 to 3 is WAW; both are name conflicts and both disappear once instruction 3 writes a different physical register.
L4.explanation: After renaming, instruction 3 can issue and even complete before instruction 2 has read its operand, because instruction 2 reads the old physical register while 3 writes a new one. That is precisely the freedom out-of-order execution monetises.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {w}-wide machine has one memory port. Two loads in the same cycle stall. Which hazard class is this, and which of the three classes does renaming NOT help with?
options: Structural; renaming helps with none of the three
Structural; renaming does not help with structural or control hazards
Data; renaming removes it
L4.answer: Structural; renaming does not help with structural or control hazards
L4.explanation: Renaming addresses WAR and WAW only. Port contention is fixed by adding ports or by scheduling, and control hazards by prediction. Knowing which mechanism answers which hazard is the point of the taxonomy.

L0.body:
# Without forwarding: the result must reach WB before ID can read it.
add r1, r2, r3
nop
nop
sub r4, r1, r5      # 2 bubbles

# With EX-to-EX forwarding: ALU result is bypassed straight to the next EX.
add r1, r2, r3
sub r4, r1, r5      # 0 bubbles

# Load-use: the value only exists at the end of MEM, one stage too late.
ld  r1, 0(r6)
sub r4, r1, r5      # 1 bubble, even with full forwarding

# Fix: schedule an independent instruction into the gap.
ld  r1, 0(r6)
add r7, r8, r9      # fills the slot
sub r4, r1, r5
L0.cloze:
Forwarding sends a result from the end of {{c1::EX}} to the input of the next {{c2::EX}}, skipping the register file.
A load-use pair still costs {{c3::1}} bubble because the loaded value is not ready until the end of {{c4::MEM}}.

concepts.L1: Bypass paths route a result from where it is produced directly to where it is consumed, instead of waiting for it to be written to and read back from the register file. Most RAW hazards then cost nothing.
concepts.L2: Forwarding does not make load-use free. On a modern out-of-order core the visible number is L1 load-use latency: about 4 to 5 cycles on recent x86, not 1, and it is the single most important latency in pointer-chasing code. Confirm it on your part rather than quoting a textbook number.
concepts.L3: Forwarding works when the producer finishes no later than the consumer needs it. ALU-to-ALU satisfies this: the result exists at the end of EX and the next EX begins the following cycle. Loads do not: the value appears at the end of MEM, one cycle after the dependent EX would have needed it, so the hardware must interlock for one cycle. Modern cores hide the same structure at a larger scale. Chasing a linked list therefore costs one full load-use latency per node with nothing to overlap, which is why pointer-heavy structures lose to arrays even at equal asymptotic complexity.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linked list of {n} nodes is traversed by pointer chasing. Every node hits in L1 with a load-use latency of {L} cycles and there is nothing else to overlap. How many cycles does the traversal take, and what is the effective IPC if each node costs 3 instructions? Answer with the number of cycles.
L4.answer: cycles $= n \cdot L$; IPC $= 3n/(nL) = 3/L$. For $n=1000, L=4$: 4000 cycles, IPC $=0.75$ on a machine that can retire 4 or more per cycle.
L4.explanation: The dependence chain, not the instruction count, sets the time. A core capable of 4 to 6 instructions per cycle delivers under 1 here, and the only fixes are to shorten the chain or to create independent chains. This is the same argument as multiple accumulators.

L4.prompt_tpl: Full forwarding removes the bubble for an ALU-to-ALU dependence but not for a load-to-ALU dependence separated by {gap} instructions when {gap} is 0. Explain why in terms of when each value exists.
L4.answer: An ALU result exists at the end of EX, and the consumer's EX starts the next cycle, so a wire suffices. A load's value only exists at the end of MEM, which is the same cycle the consumer's EX runs, so no wire can deliver it in time and the hardware must insert one stall cycle.
L4.explanation: Forwarding can move a value across space but not backwards in time. Whenever the producer's completion stage is later than the consumer's use stage, a stall is structurally required, and the scheduler's job becomes finding independent work to fill it.

concepts.t: Superscalar issue width and execution ports

L0.body:
# what the scheduler can actually start in one cycle
perf stat -e uops_dispatched.port_0,uops_dispatched.port_2,uops_dispatched.port_5 ./a.out

# Skylake-class layout, as an example only -- check uops.info for your part:
#   port 0  ALU, FMA/vector FP, branch
#   port 1  ALU, FMA/vector FP, integer multiply
#   port 5  ALU, vector shuffle
#   port 6  ALU, primary branch port
#   ports 2,3  address generation + load
#   port 4  store data,  port 7  store address
# => 2 vector FMAs per cycle, 2 loads + 1 store per cycle
L0.cloze:
Issue width is an upper bound; the real limit is the number of {{c1::ports}} that can execute your particular mix.
A loop of pure FMAs on a Skylake-class core is capped at {{c2::2}} per cycle even on a 4-wide machine.

concepts.L1: A superscalar core fetches, renames and retires several instructions per cycle. Recent x86 cores rename 4 to 6 micro-ops per cycle and retire 6 to 8; Apple and recent Arm cores are wider still. Execution happens on a set of specialised ports.
concepts.L2: Width is not the binding constraint in most loops. Ports are. Two loads per cycle, one store, two FP FMAs: if your loop needs three loads per iteration you are load-port bound no matter how wide the front end is, and no amount of unrolling helps.
concepts.L3: Model a loop body as a bag of micro-ops assigned to ports, and the steady-state cycles per iteration is at least the maximum over ports of (micro-ops on that port) divided by (copies of that port). Take a dot product on a Skylake-class core: per element two loads, one FMA. Load pressure is $2/2 = 1$ cycle per element, FMA pressure $1/2 = 0.5$: the loop is load-port bound at one element per cycle, and doubling the FMA units would change nothing. This port model, fed by the tables at uops.info or Agner Fog's instruction tables, predicts throughput of straight-line loops to within a few percent, and it is the first calculation to do before optimising.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop body issues {ld} loads, {st} stores and {fma} FMAs per iteration on a core with 2 load ports, 1 store-data port and 2 FMA ports. Give the port-limited lower bound on cycles per iteration.
L4.answer: $\max(ld/2,\; st/1,\; fma/2)$. For $ld=3, st=1, fma=2$: $\max(1.5, 1, 1) = 1.5$ cycles per iteration.
L4.explanation: The bound is a max, not a sum, because ports run in parallel. It is a lower bound only: dependence chains, front-end limits and cache misses can all push you above it, and if you are far above it the port model tells you the bottleneck is elsewhere.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your loop runs at {c} cycles per iteration and the port model predicts {p}. Which hypothesis do you test first?
options: Increase issue width by using wider instructions
You are not port bound: look for a dependence chain, a cache miss, or a front-end limit
Unroll further until the measurement matches the model
L4.answer: You are not port bound: look for a dependence chain, a cache miss, or a front-end limit
L4.explanation: Running far above the port bound means execution resources are idle, so the constraint is elsewhere. Top-down analysis will separate front-end, bad speculation and backend memory in one command, which is faster than guessing.

L0.body:
# In-order issue, out-of-order execute, in-order retire.
#
#  decode/rename -> [ scheduler / reservation stations ] -> ports -> [ ROB ] -> retire
#
# 1. rename architectural regs to physical regs   (kills WAR and WAW)
# 2. park the uop in the scheduler until its operands are ready
# 3. wake it when a producer broadcasts its tag; select among ready uops
# 4. execute in whatever order operands and ports allow
# 5. retire strictly in program order from the reorder buffer
L0.cloze:
Issue is {{c1::in order}}, execution is {{c2::out of order}}, retirement is {{c3::in order}}.
A uop leaves the scheduler when its {{c4::operands}} are ready and a port is free, not when its turn comes.

concepts.L1: Tomasulo's mechanism: rename away false dependences, hold instructions in a scheduler until their operands broadcast as ready, then execute whichever ready instruction a free port can take. Program order is restored only at retirement.
concepts.L2: Out-of-order is a latency-hiding machine, not a parallelism machine. It finds independent work to run while something stalls. If your code is one long dependence chain there is nothing independent to find, and a 512-entry window buys you exactly nothing.
concepts.L3: The scheduler is a wakeup-select loop. Each waiting micro-op holds tags for the physical registers it needs; when a result is produced its tag is broadcast, matching operands are marked ready, and the select logic picks among ready micro-ops for each port. One consequence matters most: the useful window is bounded by how many independent micro-ops fit in the scheduler and reorder buffer: reorder buffers ran about 224 entries on Skylake, about 512 on Golden Cove, about 320 on Zen 4 and larger still on Apple's cores, so check your generation. Out-of-order buys overlap; it never shortens the critical path.

L4.prompt_tpl: A core has a {rob}-entry reorder buffer. A load misses to DRAM and takes {lat} cycles. Explain why the window size determines whether that miss is hidden, and what happens when the window fills.
L4.answer: The miss is hidden only while independent micro-ops behind it keep executing. If the core sustains roughly one to four micro-ops per cycle, a 512-entry window covers a few hundred cycles of work at best. Once the buffer fills, no new micro-op can be renamed, issue stops entirely, and the core stalls until the missing load returns and retirement drains.
L4.explanation: This is why memory-level parallelism matters more than window size: two independent misses overlap and cost one latency, while two dependent misses cost two. The window sets how far ahead you can look for that second miss.

L4.prompt_tpl: Loop A is a single {n}-element dependent accumulation. Loop B is the same arithmetic split into 4 independent accumulators. Both have identical instruction counts. Why does out-of-order execution help B and not A?
L4.answer: A's every add depends on the previous add's result, so the scheduler never has two adds ready at once: throughput equals one add per adder latency. B has four chains that are mutually independent, so four adds are ready every cycle and the same adders are kept busy, giving close to a fourfold speedup on identical instruction count.
L4.explanation: Out-of-order hardware can only reorder work that is genuinely independent. Creating that independence is the programmer's job; the hardware exploits it but cannot manufacture it. This is the core lesson of dependency-chain thinking.

concepts.t: Register renaming and the physical register file

L0.body:
# Architectural names are few (16 GPRs on x86-64). Physical registers are many.
#
#  add rax, rbx     ->   p37 = p12 + p20     ; rax now maps to p37
#  mov rax, [rdi]   ->   p41 = load(p8)      ; rax now maps to p41  (WAW gone)
#  add rcx, rax     ->   p42 = p19 + p41     ; reads the CURRENT map
#
# xor eax, eax   is recognised as a zeroing idiom: renamed to a zero register,
# consumes no execution port at all on many cores. So is  sub eax, eax.
L0.cloze:
Renaming maps a small set of {{c1::architectural}} registers onto a large set of {{c2::physical}} registers.
It eliminates {{c3::WAR}} and {{c4::WAW}} hazards entirely, leaving only true {{c5::RAW}} dependences.
`xor eax, eax` is a {{c6::zeroing idiom}} handled at rename with no execution.

concepts.L1: Every write to an architectural register allocates a fresh physical register and updates a rename map. Readers consult the map at decode time, so they capture the correct version regardless of what executes when.
concepts.L2: Renaming is also where several instructions vanish entirely. Register-to-register moves, zeroing idioms and some sign extensions are resolved at rename and never occupy a port, so instruction counts overstate work. Counting instructions in a disassembly listing is not counting cost.
concepts.L3: The rename map is a table from architectural name to physical register. When `mov rax,[rdi]` renames, it allocates a new physical register for `rax`; the previous mapping stays alive for any older instruction that still needs it. WAW disappears because the two writes go to different physical registers, and WAR disappears because the older reader holds a tag pointing at the older physical register. Move elimination and zeroing idioms fall out of the same machinery, since the answer is known without executing anything. This is why `xor eax,eax` remains idiomatic over `mov eax,0`.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a core with move elimination and zeroing idioms, how many execution-port micro-ops does this sequence dispatch: `xor eax, eax` / `mov ebx, eax` / `add ecx, {k}`?
L4.answer: 1. The xor is a zeroing idiom resolved at rename, the register-to-register move is eliminated at rename on cores that support move elimination, and only the add reaches a port. Verify on your part with uops_dispatched counters, since idiom coverage differs by generation.
L4.explanation: Instruction count is 3, port pressure is 1. This gap is why IPC above the nominal issue width is possible and why comparing two versions by instruction count is unreliable. Measure micro-ops dispatched, not instructions retired.

L4.prompt_tpl: Renaming removes WAR and WAW. Explain why a machine with {arch} architectural registers and {phys} physical registers can still stall at rename.
L4.answer: Every in-flight write holds a physical register until the instruction that overwrote it retires. With enough instructions in flight the free list empties, and rename stalls until retirement frees entries. The physical register file is therefore a window limiter alongside the reorder buffer and the scheduler.
L4.explanation: In practice the binding limiter varies by workload: vector-heavy code exhausts vector physical registers first, load-heavy code exhausts load-buffer entries. Top-down analysis at level 2 reports which structure filled.

concepts.t: The reorder buffer and precise exceptions

L0.body:
# Execution finishes out of order; ARCHITECTURAL state changes in order.
#
#   ld   r1, [r2]     <-- misses to DRAM, still pending
#   add  r3, r4, r5   <-- executes and completes NOW
#   div  r6, r7, r8   <-- raises divide-by-zero
#
# The ROB holds all three in program order. The add's result sits in its
# physical register but is not architecturally visible. When the ld finally
# returns and retires, the div is at the head: the fault is taken with
# architectural state exactly as if nothing after the ld had run.
L0.cloze:
The reorder buffer restores {{c1::program order}} at retirement.
A fault is taken only when the faulting instruction reaches the {{c2::head}} of the ROB, which is what makes exceptions {{c3::precise}}.

concepts.L1: A circular buffer holding every in-flight instruction in program order. Results are committed to architectural state only from the head, in order, so the machine can always name a single instruction boundary at which state is consistent.
concepts.L2: Precise exceptions are the reason out-of-order execution is invisible to software, and the reason speculation is architecturally safe but not microarchitecturally safe. The ROB rolls back registers; it does not roll back cache state, which is the entire Spectre premise.
concepts.L3: Retirement in order gives a clean contract: for any interrupt, page fault or branch misprediction, there exists a program-order point where everything before it is complete and nothing after it is visible. Implementation follows: results go to physical registers on completion, the ROB entry is marked done, and only at retirement does the rename map's committed copy advance. Flush is cheap because it is a pointer reset plus map restore. The gap is that the ROB tracks architectural state only. A speculatively executed load that filled a cache line leaves that line filled after the flush, and no rollback removes it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Instruction {i} raises a page fault but instruction {j} (later in program order) has already executed and produced a result. Explain how the machine still delivers a precise fault.
L4.answer: Instruction j's result lives only in a physical register and its ROB entry; it has not been committed. Retirement is in order, so when i reaches the ROB head the fault is signalled, every younger entry including j is squashed, the rename map is restored to its committed state, and the handler sees architectural state as of just before i.
L4.explanation: Out-of-order completion plus in-order retirement is the whole trick. It is also the exact boundary Spectre attacks: register state rolls back, cache and predictor state do not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A speculatively executed load reads a secret and uses it to index an array, touching cache line {n}. The branch then mispredicts and the ROB squashes everything. What has the ROB restored and what has it not?
L4.answer: Restored: architectural registers, the rename map, the program counter, and memory, since no store retired. Not restored: the cache line that was filled, TLB entries touched, branch predictor and prefetcher state. An attacker times access to each candidate line and reads the secret out of the timing.
L4.explanation: The ISA promises a register and memory state machine and says nothing about timing. That omission is structural, not a bug, which is why mitigations are a permanent tax rather than a patch.

With $c$ around 15 to 20 cycles and $d$ around 1 to 3, the crossover sits near $p$ of a few percent — so a branch mispredicting 1 percent of the time should stay a branch, and one at 30 percent should not. Both $c$ and the predictor's accuracy are generation-dependent, so measure the crossover on your hardware rather than trusting the estimate.

concepts.L1: Spectre and Meltdown exploit the fact that speculative execution leaves microarchitectural traces even when architecturally rolled back.
concepts.L2: The deep point: the ISA is not a complete specification of observable behavior. Timing is a side channel the architecture never promised to hide, and that's a permanent structural issue, not a bug that got patched.
concepts.L3: The attacker trains the branch to be taken, evicts `array1_size` so resolving the condition takes hundreds of cycles, then supplies an out-of-bounds `i`. The core predicts taken and, during the resolution window, issues both loads: one reads out-of-bounds memory, the second uses that byte to index `array2` and fills exactly one of 256 lines. The branch resolves, the ROB squashes both loads, and registers and memory are clean. The attacker then times a read of each of the 256 candidate lines; the fast one names the byte. The mitigations are structural — index masking, `lfence`, retpolines, process isolation — because there is no patch for the fact that timing was never part of the contract.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why adding a second bounds check after the first, or asserting `i < {n}` again inside the branch, does not mitigate Spectre v1.
L4.answer: Both checks are branches, and both are predicted. Speculation proceeds past the second check for the same reason it passed the first, so the out-of-bounds load still issues and still leaves its cache trace. The fix must make the speculative address safe regardless of prediction: mask the index into range, or place a barrier that blocks speculative issue.
L4.explanation: The bug is not a missing check. It is that checks are branches and branches are predicted. Only data dependences on the index, or an explicit serialising barrier, constrain the speculative path.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is the multiplier {m} used when indexing the probe array in the classic Spectre proof of concept?
L4.answer: It spreads the 256 possible secret values across distinct cache lines, and usually distinct pages, so that each candidate is separately measurable and the hardware prefetcher does not pull in neighbours and blur the signal. A stride of 512 or 4096 bytes puts each candidate well beyond one 64-byte line.
L4.explanation: The covert channel needs one resolvable bucket per secret value. Too small a stride and adjacent values share a line or get prefetched together, destroying the resolution of the timing measurement.

One accumulator is bound by FP add {{c1::latency}}; four accumulators are bound by adder {{c2::throughput}}.
The compiler will not do this automatically because FP addition is not {{c3::associative}}.

concepts.L1: The limit on throughput is usually the critical dependency chain, not the instruction count. Unrolling with multiple accumulators breaks the chain and can give near-linear speedup on reduction loops.
concepts.L2: A summation loop with one accumulator is latency-bound on the adder. Four independent accumulators run four times faster on the same instruction count. This is a concrete, demonstrable trick most engineers have never seen.
concepts.L3: Take the throughput bound directly from the hardware. Let $L$ be the dependent latency of the accumulate operation and $T$ its reciprocal throughput. A single chain runs at $L$ cycles per element because each add waits on the previous one. With $k$ independent accumulators, $k$ adds are in flight and the loop runs at $\max(L/k,\, T)$ cycles per element. Speedup saturates at $k = L/T$: on a core with FP add latency 4 and two add units ($T = 0.5$), the ideal is $k = 8$, and going beyond that only burns registers. Measure $L$ and $T$ for your operation in the instruction tables, then unroll to $L/T$.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accumulate operation has dependent latency {L} cycles and reciprocal throughput {T} cycles. With {k} independent accumulators, give cycles per element and the number of accumulators beyond which there is no further gain. Answer with the cycles per element.
L4.answer: cycles per element $= \max(L/k,\, T)$; saturation at $k = L/T$. For $L=4, T=0.5, k=4$: $\max(1.0, 0.5) = 1.0$ cycles; saturation at $k=8$ giving 0.5.
L4.explanation: Below saturation you are latency-bound and each extra accumulator helps proportionally. Above it you are throughput-bound and extra accumulators only increase register pressure, which can spill and make things worse. Compute $L/T$ before choosing an unroll factor.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague reports that adding {k} accumulators to a `double` summation gave no speedup at all under `-O2`, but a large one under `-O3 -ffast-math`. What happened, and what silently changed?
L4.answer: Under -O2 the compiler could not vectorise or reassociate the original single-chain loop, so their hand-written version was the only source of parallelism and should have helped; if it did not, the accumulators were merged back or the loop was memory-bound. Under -ffast-math the compiler is permitted to reassociate and vectorise, which is where the speedup came from. What changed silently is numerical semantics: summation order changed, so results differ, and the change is not bit-reproducible.
L4.explanation: Reassociation is a correctness decision, not an optimisation flag to set reflexively. In reductions over large arrays, pairwise or Kahan summation may be both faster and more accurate than a naive single chain, so state the accuracy requirement first.

concepts.L1: SSE, AVX2, AVX-512, ARM NEON and SVE. Auto-vectorization when the compiler can prove independence and alignment; intrinsics when it can't.
concepts.L2: AVX-512 causes frequency throttling on many Intel parts, so a vectorized loop can slow down the rest of the program. This is a real and widely-missed effect.
concepts.L3: Vectorisation multiplies work per instruction, so it only helps where you were compute-limited or where you were paying per-element overhead. A memory-bound loop at 0.1 FLOP per byte gains nothing from doubling vector width, because the bottleneck is bytes moved. Decide with the roofline first. Then the mechanical requirements: the compiler must prove the iterations are independent, which usually means no aliasing (add `restrict` or `__restrict`) and no loop-carried dependence; and for FP reductions it must be allowed to reassociate. Intrinsics are the fallback, and they cost portability: an AVX-512 kernel needs a NEON or SVE sibling.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop does {f} FLOPs per element on {b}-byte elements and is memory bound. You move from {w1}-bit to {w2}-bit vectors. What speedup should you expect, and why?
L4.answer: Roughly none. Arithmetic intensity is unchanged at $f/(\text{bytes moved})$, and a memory-bound kernel's time is set by bytes divided by achievable bandwidth. Wider vectors issue the same bytes in fewer instructions but the bytes still have to cross the same bus. Expect a small gain from reduced instruction and loop overhead only.
L4.explanation: Widening helps only above the roofline ridge point. Below it, the fix is to move fewer bytes: fuse, change layout, or improve reuse. This is the single most common misallocation of optimisation effort.

L4.prompt_tpl: `void add(float *a, float *b, float *c, int n){{ for(int i=0;i<{n};i++) c[i]=a[i]+b[i]; }}` is not vectorised. Give the reason and the one-word fix.
L4.answer: The compiler cannot prove that c does not alias a or b, so a store to c[i] might change a[i+1]. It emits a runtime alias check with a scalar fallback, or scalar code outright. Fix: declare the pointers restrict, or pass non-overlapping guarantees another way.
L4.explanation: Aliasing is the number one cause of failed auto-vectorisation in C and C++. Fortran vectorises more readily precisely because its arrays are assumed non-aliasing by the standard, which is most of the historical performance gap.

concepts.L1: Two logical threads sharing execution resources. Helps when threads stall on memory; hurts when both are compute-bound and contend for the same ports.
concepts.L2: For latency-critical services, SMT is often disabled deliberately — it improves throughput and worsens tail latency by making per-thread performance variable.
concepts.L3: SMT duplicates architectural state (registers, program counter, rename map) but shares the expensive parts: execution ports, L1 and L2, the branch predictor, the TLB. Whether that helps depends entirely on whether the shared resources are saturated. Two memory-bound threads interleave usefully because each spends most cycles waiting; the second thread fills the idle ports for free. Two FMA-bound threads simply queue for the same units, so aggregate throughput barely moves while each thread's latency roughly doubles. Typical reported gains are in the 10 to 30 percent range on throughput workloads and negative on latency ones; measure both p50 and p99 with SMT on and off before deciding.

L4.prompt_tpl: With SMT off, a service holds p50 {p50}ms and p99 {p99}ms at throughput {tp} rps. With SMT on, throughput rises {gain} percent but p99 rises {p99gain} percent. If your SLO is a p99 under {slo}ms, is SMT acceptable?

Throughput gain is irrelevant if the SLO is breached, because you must then run below capacity anyway.
L4.explanation: SMT trades a variance increase for a throughput increase. That trade is good for batch and bad for tail-bound services. Frame it as a constraint problem, not an optimisation, and measure your own numbers because the gains vary hugely by workload.

Dense FMA: almost no gain, since both saturate the same FP units, and each thread's own latency roughly doubles. Versus two separate physical cores, SMT is always worse or equal in throughput; the question is whether it beats leaving the sibling idle.
L4.explanation: SMT harvests stall cycles. Its value is exactly the fraction of cycles the first thread leaves the shared units idle, which is why it shines on memory-bound and branch-mispredicting code and does nothing for compute-saturated kernels.

concepts.t: The load-store queue and memory disambiguation

L0.body:
store [rdi], rax        ; address of rdi not yet computed
load  rbx, [rsi]        ; may or may not alias -- the core must guess

; The load queue and store queue track every in-flight memory op.
; Store-to-load forwarding: a load fully covered by an older store in the
; store buffer gets its data from there, no cache access needed.
;
; Fails and costs 10+ extra cycles when the load is only PARTIALLY covered:
mov  word  [rdi], ax    ; 2-byte store
mov  ebx,  [rdi]        ; 4-byte load overlapping it -> stall, no forwarding
L0.cloze:
A load fully covered by an older store is served by {{c1::store-to-load forwarding}}.
A {{c2::partially}} overlapping load cannot be forwarded and stalls.
Guessing wrong about aliasing triggers a {{c3::memory order machine clear}}.

concepts.L1: Loads and stores are tracked in queues so the core can execute them out of order while preserving the illusion of program order. A load may be speculatively issued before an older store whose address is unknown; if they turn out to alias, the machine squashes and replays.
concepts.L2: The interesting failure is not the alias but the forwarding shape. A load that overlaps an older store only partially, or that crosses the store's boundary, cannot be forwarded and pays a large penalty. Type-punned unions and byte-wise buffer writes followed by word reads hit this constantly.
concepts.L3: The core keeps a store buffer of retired-but-not-yet-committed stores. If exactly one older store fully contains the load's bytes and is aligned compatibly, the data is forwarded in a few cycles and the cache is never touched. If the coverage is partial, or several stores contribute, the hardware waits for the stores to drain to L1 and then reloads, which on Intel parts has been measured at roughly 10 to 15 extra cycles. Separately, the core predicts whether a load aliases an older store with an unknown address. A wrong guess is a memory order machine clear, more expensive than a branch misprediction because the whole pipeline is flushed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A serialiser writes {n} individual bytes into a buffer and then reads them back as 4-byte words. It is unexpectedly slow. Name the microarchitectural event and the counter you would confirm it with.
L4.answer: Failed store-to-load forwarding: each 4-byte load overlaps several narrower stores, none of which fully covers it, so the load must wait for the store buffer to drain to L1. Confirm with ld_blocks.store_forward on Intel, or the equivalent store-forwarding-block counter on your part.
L4.explanation: The fix is to make widths match: build the word in a register and store it once, or read back at the same granularity you wrote. Byte-at-a-time write followed by word-at-a-time read is a very common pattern in parsers and serialisers.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is a memory order machine clear typically more expensive than a branch misprediction of {c} cycles?
L4.answer: A branch misprediction redirects fetch and squashes younger work, but the predictor recovers using structures designed for it. A memory order violation is detected late, at the point the offending store's address resolves, and forces a full pipeline clear plus a restart from the load, with no fast recovery path. Reported costs are commonly higher than a branch flush, and it also poisons the memory dependence predictor.
L4.explanation: Both are speculation failures, but the recovery machinery differs. This is why alias-heavy code with unpredictable pointer relationships is slow in a way profilers attribute to Bad Speculation rather than to memory.

concepts.t: Bimodal prediction and the saturating counter

L0.body:
# 2-bit saturating counter per branch, indexed by PC bits
#
#   00 strongly-not-taken  <-- 01 weakly-not-taken
#   10 weakly-taken        --> 11 strongly-taken
#
#   taken     : counter = min(counter + 1, 3)
#   not taken : counter = max(counter - 1, 0)
#   predict taken iff counter >= 2
#
# A loop of N iterations: 1-bit predictor mispredicts 2 per execution
# (the exit, then the first iteration of the next entry).
# 2-bit predictor mispredicts 1 per execution: hysteresis absorbs the exit.
L0.cloze:
A 2-bit counter predicts taken iff counter $\geq$ {{c1::2}}.
Its extra bit provides {{c2::hysteresis}}, so one anomalous outcome does not flip the prediction.
Over a loop executed repeatedly, this halves mispredictions from {{c3::2}} to {{c4::1}} per execution.

concepts.L1: The baseline predictor: a table of two-bit saturating counters indexed by branch address. Increment on taken, decrement on not-taken, predict taken at 2 or 3. It captures per-branch bias and nothing else.
concepts.L2: The second bit is not for precision, it is for hysteresis. A one-bit predictor mispredicts twice per loop execution rather than once, because after the exit it has learned the wrong thing for the next entry. Two bits absorb single anomalies at the cost of being slower to adapt to genuine change.
concepts.L3: Work the loop case. A loop body branch executed $N$ times per entry is taken $N-1$ times and not taken once. With one bit, the exit mispredicts, the state flips to not-taken, and then the first iteration of the next entry mispredicts too: two per entry, so accuracy $1 - 2/N$. With two bits at strongly-taken, the exit decrements to weakly-taken and still predicts taken next time, so only the exit mispredicts: accuracy $1 - 1/N$. The remaining weakness is that a bimodal predictor has no notion of correlation. That gap is what global history predictors and then TAGE exist to close.

L4.prompt_tpl: An inner loop of {N} iterations is entered {E} times. Give the misprediction count and rate for a 1-bit predictor and for a 2-bit saturating counter, ignoring warm-up. Answer with the 1-bit predictor's misprediction count.
L4.answer: 1-bit: $2E$ mispredictions, rate $2/N$. 2-bit: $E$ mispredictions, rate $1/N$. For $N=100, E=1000$: 2000 versus 1000 mispredictions, rates 2 percent and 1 percent.
L4.explanation: Short inner loops are where this matters. At $N=10$ a 2-bit predictor still mispredicts 10 percent of the time, which at 15 to 20 cycles a flush is a real cost — one reason unrolling a short loop can pay for itself in prediction alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: A branch follows the exact repeating pattern of period {p}: T, N, T, N, ... What accuracy does a 2-bit bimodal counter reach in steady state, and what minimal extra state would make it perfect?
L4.answer: About 50 percent: the counter oscillates around the weak states and gets roughly half wrong. One bit of global or local branch history, used to index two separate counters, predicts it perfectly, since the outcome is a deterministic function of the previous outcome.
L4.explanation: This is the argument for history-based prediction in one example. Bimodal captures bias; correlation needs history. TAGE generalises it by keeping many history lengths at once and choosing the longest one that matches.

L0.body:
# TAGE = TAgged GEometric history length predictor  (Seznec, 2006)
#
#   T0 : untagged bimodal base predictor            (always hits)
#   T1 : tagged, history length  h1 =  2
#   T2 : tagged, history length  h2 =  4
#   T3 : tagged, history length  h3 =  8
#   ...   h_i grows GEOMETRICALLY: h_i = h_1 * r^(i-1)
#
# predict: use the entry from the LONGEST history length whose TAG matches
# update : on a misprediction, allocate an entry in a table with a LONGER
#          history than the one that provided the wrong prediction
L0.cloze:
TAGE keeps several tagged tables indexed by histories of {{c1::geometrically}} increasing length.
It predicts from the {{c2::longest}} matching table and falls back to a {{c3::bimodal}} base predictor.
On a misprediction it allocates in a table with a {{c4::longer}} history.

concepts.L1: Seznec's design: many predictor tables, each indexed by a hash of the branch address with a different length of global history, lengths growing geometrically. Tags let a table say it has no opinion, so the longest table that recognises the situation wins.
concepts.L2: The geometric spacing is the whole idea. Branches correlate at wildly different distances, from 2 to hundreds of branches back, and a linear set of lengths wastes most of its tables on a narrow band. Geometric spacing covers several orders of magnitude with a handful of tables.
concepts.L3: A fixed-history predictor faces an impossible tuning problem: short histories cannot capture long-range correlation, long histories dilute simple biased branches across enormous index spaces and take forever to train. TAGE sidesteps it by asking every length at once and trusting the longest one that has actually seen this exact history, which the tag check verifies. Consequences for you: a branch is predictable if its outcome is a function of recent branch history, even a long and complicated one, and unpredictable mainly when it depends on data the history does not encode, like a hash of an incoming key.

L4.prompt_tpl: Table {i} in a TAGE predictor uses history length {h}. Explain why a set of lengths spaced geometrically outperforms the same number of tables spaced linearly.
L4.answer: Correlation distances in real code span several orders of magnitude. Linear spacing, say 8, 16, 24, 32, covers one narrow band and leaves both short-range bias and long-range correlation unserved. Geometric spacing, say 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256, covers the whole range with the same table count, which matters because tables are the expensive resource.
L4.explanation: This is a resource allocation argument, not a statistical one. Given a fixed silicon budget of tables, geometric spacing maximises the range of correlation structures any one of them can capture.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hash table probe branches on whether a key matched. With {n} random keys, the branch mispredicts near 50 percent. Would a better predictor fix it?
options: Yes: a longer history length would eventually capture the pattern
No: the outcome depends on data the branch history does not encode, so it is irreducibly unpredictable and the fix is to remove the branch
Yes: TAGE allocates on misprediction so it converges on any pattern
L4.answer: No: the outcome depends on data the branch history does not encode, so it is irreducibly unpredictable and the fix is to remove the branch
L4.explanation: Predictors learn functions of past control flow. When the outcome is a function of input data with no control-flow correlate, no predictor helps, and the branchless rewrite becomes the right answer. This is exactly the crossover the branch-prediction concept computes.

concepts.L1: An indirect branch has no target encoded in the instruction, so the front end must predict where to fetch from. The branch target buffer caches recent targets by branch address; ITTAGE-style predictors extend it with global history to disambiguate polymorphic sites.
concepts.L2: Megamorphic call sites are not slow because of the indirection but because of prediction failure. A virtual call with one implementation is essentially free; the same call site with twenty implementations in random order mispredicts constantly. Devirtualisation is a prediction fix, not a call-overhead fix.
concepts.L3: Two structures matter. Indirect target predictors add history so that the same call site can predict differently depending on the path that reached it, which is why a monomorphic-per-path interpreter loop predicts far better than a single shared dispatch. The return stack buffer, commonly 16 to 32 entries, predicts `ret` by popping what `call` pushed; deep recursion overflows it and stack-switching runtimes (coroutines, fibers, setjmp) desynchronise it, producing a burst of mispredictions with no obvious source in the code. Bytecode interpreters exploit this by replicating the dispatch jump at the end of every handler, giving each opcode its own BTB entry and its own history.

L4.prompt_tpl: An interpreter's main loop ends with one shared `switch` dispatch. Replicating the dispatch into the tail of each of the {k} opcode handlers speeds it up substantially with the same instruction count. Why?
L4.answer: One shared indirect jump gives the predictor a single site whose target sequence is the whole bytecode stream, which is close to random. Replicating it gives each opcode its own branch site, so the predictor learns per-opcode successor distributions, which in real bytecode are strongly biased. Target misprediction rate falls sharply.
L4.explanation: This is threaded interpretation, and it is a branch prediction optimisation rather than a code-size one. The gain shrinks on cores with strong history-based indirect predictors, which is a good example of a technique whose value is generation-dependent.

L4.prompt_tpl: A coroutine runtime switches stacks {n} times per second and profiles show a spike in branch mispredictions with no branchy code. What structure is being corrupted, and why?
L4.answer: The return stack buffer. It is a hardware stack pushed by call and popped by ret; switching stacks means subsequent rets pop predictions belonging to a different call chain, so every return in the resumed context mispredicts until the RSB refills.
L4.explanation: The same effect appears with setjmp/longjmp, exception unwinding and hand-rolled context switches. It is invisible in source and shows up in perf as branch-misses on ret instructions, which is a diagnostic worth recognising.

L0.body:
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,branches,branch-misses,\
              topdown-bad-spec ./a.out

#  misprediction rate = branch-misses / branches
#  cycles lost        ~ branch-misses * penalty
#  penalty            = pipeline refill depth, ~15-20 cycles on recent x86
#                       -- MEASURE it, do not assume

# The published penalty assumes the condition is already available.
# If the branch depends on a load that misses to DRAM, the real cost is
# the miss latency, because resolution cannot happen until the data arrives.
L0.cloze:
Misprediction rate is `{{c1::branch-misses / branches}}`.
The refill penalty is roughly {{c2::15-20}} cycles on recent x86, but that assumes the condition is {{c3::already available}}.
A branch on a DRAM-missing load costs the {{c4::miss latency}} instead.

concepts.L1: The published penalty is the front-end refill: the cycles between discovering the wrong target and re-filling the pipeline with correct instructions. On recent x86 cores that is roughly 15 to 20 cycles, and it scales with pipeline depth, so it differs by generation.
concepts.L2: The refill number is a floor, not the cost. The real cost is how long resolution took, which is the latency of whatever the condition depends on. A branch on a cache-missing load holds the wrong path live for hundreds of cycles, and all that work is discarded.
concepts.L3: Refill is architectural and roughly fixed per core, around 15 to 20 cycles on recent x86 designs; confirm yours with a microbenchmark that alternates predictable and random branches and differences the cycle counts. Detection delay is the time from issuing the branch to resolving it, which equals the latency of its input chain. If it is `if (node->key == k)` where `node` just missed to DRAM, resolution waits 200 to 300 cycles, and every micro-op issued down the wrong path in that window is wasted work and wasted power. This is why mispredictions and cache misses compound rather than add, and why top-down analysis reports Bad Speculation and Memory Bound as separate but interacting buckets.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program executes {b} branches with a {r} percent misprediction rate on a core with a {c}-cycle refill penalty, in {cyc} total cycles. What fraction of cycles is lost to refill alone? Answer with the fraction of cycles lost to refill.
L4.answer: lost $= b \cdot (r/100) \cdot c$; fraction $= $ lost $/ cyc$. For $b=10^{9}$, $r=5$, $c=20$, $cyc=3\times10^{9}$: $10^{9}$ cycles lost, i.e. 33 percent.
L4.explanation: This is a floor: it counts refill only and ignores the wasted work issued before resolution. If top-down reports Bad Speculation well above this number, the extra is detection delay, which means the branch conditions themselves are waiting on memory.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two branches both mispredict {r} percent of the time. Branch A's condition compares two registers; branch B's condition depends on a load that misses to DRAM at {lat} cycles. Explain why B costs far more, and what the extra cost consists of.
L4.answer: A resolves in a cycle or two, so its cost is the refill penalty. B cannot resolve until the load returns, so for the full miss latency the core issues, executes and buffers wrong-path work that will be squashed. The extra cost is that wasted execution plus the occupancy of scheduler, ROB and load-buffer entries, which also blocks useful work from entering the window.
L4.explanation: This is why sorting data, or hoisting the loads that feed conditions, can help more than removing the branch. It shortens detection delay rather than the refill, and detection delay is the part that varies by orders of magnitude.

concepts.t: Index, tag and offset: the address split

L0.body:
# A cache is (sets x ways x line size). The address is split accordingly.
#
#   offset bits = log2(line_size)
#   index  bits = log2(num_sets),  num_sets = capacity / (line_size * ways)
#   tag    bits = address_bits - index_bits - offset_bits
#
# Worked: 32 KiB, 8-way, 64 B lines
#   sets   = 32768 / (64 * 8) = 64
#   offset = 6 bits, index = 6 bits
#   two addresses collide in the same set iff they agree in bits [11:6]
#   => conflict stride = num_sets * line_size = 64 * 64 = 4096 bytes
L0.cloze:
num_sets = capacity / (line_size * {{c1::ways}}).
For a 32 KiB 8-way cache with 64 B lines there are {{c2::64}} sets, so offset is {{c3::6}} bits and index is {{c4::6}} bits.
The stride that maps everything to one set is {{c5::4096}} bytes.

concepts.L1: Every address is cut into offset (which byte in the line), index (which set), and tag (the rest, stored to identify the line). Set count is capacity divided by line size times associativity, and that single number decides which addresses can evict each other.
concepts.L2: The important derived quantity is the conflict stride, sets times line size. On a typical 32 KiB 8-way L1 that is exactly 4096 bytes, so page-aligned buffers and power-of-two 2D array strides land in the same set and thrash an 8-way cache with nine live rows.
concepts.L3: Compute it once and it explains a class of mysteries. With 64 sets and 64-byte lines, index bits are address bits 11 through 6, so any two addresses differing only above bit 11 share a set. Allocate nine buffers each aligned to 4096 bytes and touch one element of each in a loop: all nine map to set 0, the cache is 8-way, and every access misses. The classic instance is a 2D array with a power-of-two row length: walking a column strides by a multiple of 4096 and hits one set repeatedly. The fix is to break the alignment, usually by padding the row length by one line, which costs a fraction of a percent of memory and can multiply throughput.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cache has capacity {cap} KiB, {ways}-way associativity and {line}-byte lines. Give the number of sets, the index bit count, the offset bit count, and the stride in bytes that maps all accesses to one set. Answer with the number of sets.
L4.answer: sets $= cap \cdot 1024/(line \cdot ways)$; index $= \log_{2}(sets)$; offset $= \log_{2}(line)$; stride $= sets \cdot line$. For 32 KiB, 8-way, 64 B: 64 sets, 6 index bits, 6 offset bits, stride 4096 bytes.
L4.explanation: For 48 KiB 12-way 64 B, the arithmetic also yields 64 sets and a 4096-byte stride, which is why the recent Intel and AMD L1 caches behave the same way here despite differing in size. Always compute rather than assume the stride from capacity alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}x{n} float matrix transpose is far slower than the copy of the same data. Explain in terms of the index arithmetic and give a one-line fix.
L4.answer: The row length in bytes is a large power of two, so consecutive elements of a column are separated by a multiple of the conflict stride and all map to the same set. The column walk evicts itself. Fix: pad the row length, allocating n+1 or n+8 floats per row, or tile the transpose so a block of rows and columns fits in cache.
L4.explanation: Padding costs a fraction of a percent of memory and typically restores several times the throughput. The same pattern appears in FFTs, stencils and any strided access over power-of-two dimensions, which is why tuned libraries pad their leading dimension.

L0.body:
# Miss taxonomy (Hill's three Cs), and how to separate them by experiment:
#   compulsory : still misses in an INFINITE cache          -- cold, unavoidable
#   capacity   : misses in a fully-associative cache of this size
#   conflict   : hits fully-associative, misses at this associativity
#
# Experiment: simulate/measure the same trace at
#   (a) infinite cache      -> compulsory
#   (b) same size, full assoc -> compulsory + capacity
#   (c) same size, W-way      -> all three
# conflict = (c) - (b)
L0.cloze:
The three Cs are {{c1::compulsory}}, {{c2::capacity}} and {{c3::conflict}}.
Conflict misses are exactly those that would have {{c4::hit}} in a fully associative cache of the same size.

concepts.L1: Associativity is how many lines may share one set. Direct-mapped has one, fully associative has all. It exists only to reduce conflict misses: the misses caused by unlucky address bits rather than by insufficient capacity.
concepts.L2: Going from 8-way to 16-way rarely buys much on ordinary code, which is why designers stopped there. The wins come from removing the pathological strides instead, and a padded data layout on an 8-way cache beats an unpadded one on a 16-way cache almost every time.
concepts.L3: Separate the three Cs before choosing a fix, because they need different ones. Compulsory misses shrink only by moving fewer distinct lines: compress, change layout, or fuse passes so a line is touched once. Capacity misses shrink by blocking, so the working set of the inner loop fits the level you are targeting. Conflict misses shrink by changing addresses, that is padding or offsetting allocations, and they are the ones that produce spectacular cliff-edge behaviour where a buffer one element larger runs several times faster. The practical test is cheap: change your allocation size or alignment by one cache line and re-measure. If the time moves sharply, you had conflicts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {w}-way set-associative cache is accessed cyclically over {n} distinct lines that all map to the same set, repeated many times. Give the steady-state hit rate under true LRU and say what happens if {n} is reduced to {w}. Answer with the steady-state hit rate as a percentage.
L4.answer: 0 percent. LRU evicts the line that will be needed next in a cyclic pattern of length greater than the associativity, so every access misses. Reduce n to w and the hit rate jumps to essentially 100 percent.
L4.explanation: This is LRU's pathological case and the sharpest cliff in caching. One extra live line takes you from all hits to all misses, which is why measured performance sometimes falls off a cliff at a specific working-set size rather than degrading smoothly.

L4.prompt_tpl: Adding {pad} bytes of padding to each element of an array of structs makes a loop over {n} elements faster despite moving more bytes. Which of the three Cs did you reduce?
options: Compulsory, because fewer distinct lines are now touched
Conflict, because the padding changed which set each element maps to
Capacity, because the working set now fits in cache
L4.answer: Conflict, because the padding changed which set each element maps to
L4.explanation: Padding strictly increases bytes moved, so it cannot reduce compulsory or capacity misses. If it helps, the only remaining explanation is that the previous stride was aliasing into too few sets. This is the diagnostic value of the taxonomy.

concepts.t: Replacement policy: LRU, pseudo-LRU and RRIP

L0.body:
# True LRU on a W-way set needs an ordering over W lines.
#   matrix LRU : W*W bits per set   -- 256 bits for 16-way, too expensive
#   tree PLRU  : W-1 bits per set   -- 15 bits for 16-way, one bit per node
#
# RRIP (Jaleel et al. 2010): 2-bit re-reference prediction value per line
#   0 = near-immediate reuse expected ... 3 = distant / no reuse expected
#   INSERT new lines at 2 (long, not immediate) so a streaming scan cannot
#   evict the resident working set.  Promote to 0 on a hit.
L0.cloze:
True LRU costs about {{c1::W*W}} bits per set; tree pseudo-LRU costs {{c2::W-1}} bits.
RRIP inserts new lines at a {{c3::distant}} re-reference position so that a {{c4::streaming scan}} cannot evict the working set.

concepts.L1: Which line to evict when a set is full. True LRU is the textbook answer and is rarely implemented at high associativity because the state cost grows quadratically; tree-based pseudo-LRU approximates it in $W-1$ bits, and RRIP-family policies predict reuse distance instead.
concepts.L2: LRU is not the target to approximate; it is a heuristic with a known pathology. Any access pattern that cycles over slightly more lines than the associativity gets zero hits under LRU, and random replacement beats it there. Real caches deliberately deviate from LRU, so LRU-based mental models mispredict.
concepts.L3: The failure mode is scan resistance. Under LRU, every scan line is inserted as most-recently-used and evicts a hot line; by the time the hot lines are needed again they are gone. RRIP fixes this by inserting new lines with a distant re-reference prediction, so an unre-referenced scan line is the first candidate for eviction and the working set survives. Practical consequence: you cannot reason about a modern last-level cache as if it were LRU, vendors do not document the policy, and the reliable move is to measure hit rates at each level while varying working-set size rather than predicting them from a policy model.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare state cost per set for a {w}-way cache: matrix LRU at $W^{{2}}$ bits, tree pseudo-LRU at $W-1$ bits, and RRIP at 2 bits per line. Give all three numbers. Answer with the matrix-LRU state cost in bits.
L4.answer: For $W=16$: matrix LRU 256 bits, tree PLRU 15 bits, RRIP $2 \times 16 = 32$ bits. For $W=8$: 64, 7 and 16 bits.
L4.explanation: The quadratic term is why true LRU is not built at high associativity. RRIP is cheap and also better on scan-heavy workloads, so it wins on both axes, which is the usual reason a policy displaces a textbook one.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hot working set of exactly {w} lines shares a {w}-way set with a streaming scan of {n} new lines per pass. Predict the hit rate under LRU and under an RRIP-style insertion policy.
L4.answer: Under LRU the hit rate collapses towards zero: every scan line is inserted as most-recently-used and evicts a hot line, so the working set is destroyed each pass. Under RRIP the scan lines are inserted at a distant re-reference prediction and are evicted by the next scan line, so the hot set survives and its hit rate stays near 100 percent.
L4.explanation: Scan resistance is the single biggest practical difference between real cache policies and the LRU model. It is also why a large sequential read can quietly destroy an unrelated service's cache performance on a shared last-level cache.

concepts.t: Write policy: write-back, write-allocate and write-combining

L0.cloze:
An ordinary store to an absent line costs a {{c1::read-for-ownership}}, so write-only streaming moves {{c2::2}} bytes per byte written.
Non-temporal stores avoid the RFO via a {{c3::write-combining}} buffer, but are weakly ordered and need an {{c4::sfence}}.

concepts.L1: Write-back caches hold dirty lines and write them once on eviction. Write-allocate means a store miss first fetches the line. Write-combining buffers gather full-line non-temporal stores and send them to memory without ever owning the line in cache.
concepts.L2: The hidden cost is the read-for-ownership on write-only data. A memset or a large output buffer reads every line it is about to overwrite completely, doubling bandwidth for no benefit, and non-temporal stores can recover close to the full factor on buffers larger than the last-level cache.
concepts.L3: Trace a store to a line not present in cache. Coherence requires exclusive ownership before modifying, so the line is read from memory, marked exclusive, then modified. You paid a 64-byte read to write 64 bytes you were going to overwrite entirely. For a buffer larger than the last-level cache, total traffic is roughly twice the useful bytes and effective bandwidth roughly halves. Non-temporal stores target a small set of write-combining buffers; once a buffer holds a full line it is flushed straight to memory with no ownership request and no cache pollution. Measure at your actual buffer size.

L4.prompt_tpl: You write {mb} MB of output with ordinary stores on a machine with {bw} GB/s of memory bandwidth and a last-level cache far smaller than the buffer. Give the bytes actually moved and the time, then repeat assuming non-temporal stores eliminate the read-for-ownership. Answer with the megabytes actually moved with ordinary stores.
L4.answer: Ordinary: $2 \cdot mb$ MB moved, time $= 2 \cdot mb/(bw \cdot 1000)$ seconds. NT: $mb$ MB, half the time. For 1024 MB at 100 GB/s: 2048 MB and 20.5 ms versus 1024 MB and 10.2 ms.
L4.explanation: The upper bound on the speedup is 2x and only applies when the buffer exceeds the last-level cache and lines are written in full. Achieved gains are commonly in the 1.3x to 1.8x range; measure rather than assume the ideal.

L4.prompt_tpl: A developer replaces all stores in a hot loop with `_mm256_stream_ps` and the program gets slower, and occasionally produces stale data for a reader thread on another core. Give both bugs.
L4.answer: Performance: the data is re-read shortly afterwards, and non-temporal stores bypass the cache, so every subsequent read is a full memory access. NT stores only pay off for data that will not be read soon and for buffers larger than the LLC. Correctness: NT stores are weakly ordered with respect to other stores, so a publishing flag can become visible before the data. An sfence, or a release store that implies one, is required before publication.
L4.explanation: Both mistakes are common. The ordering one is worse because it produces a rare data-dependent bug rather than a slowdown, and it will not reproduce under a debugger.

concepts.t: Cache coherence and the MESI protocol

L0.body:
# Per-line state in each core's private cache:
#   M  Modified  : dirty, this core only. Memory is stale.
#   E  Exclusive : clean, this core only. Memory is up to date.
#   S  Shared    : clean, possibly in other caches.
#   I  Invalid   : not present.
#
# read miss, no other copy      -> E     (silent upgrade to M on write: FREE)
# read miss, another copy       -> S
# write to S                    -> send Read-For-Ownership, others -> I, this -> M
# another core reads your M     -> you supply the data, both -> S (or O in MOESI)
L0.cloze:
MESI states are {{c1::Modified}}, {{c2::Exclusive}}, {{c3::Shared}}, {{c4::Invalid}}.
E exists so a private line can be written with {{c5::no bus traffic}}.
Writing a line in S requires a {{c6::read-for-ownership}} that invalidates every other copy.

concepts.L1: Hardware keeps all private caches consistent for each 64-byte line by tracking a state per line and exchanging messages. MESI is the base protocol: a write requires exclusive ownership, which invalidates every other cached copy of that line.
concepts.L2: Exclusive is the state that pays for itself. Without it, every first write to privately-owned data would broadcast an invalidation; with it, a line read by one core and then written by it upgrades silently. Most of the cost of shared-memory programming is the traffic E is designed to avoid.
concepts.L3: Coherence gives one guarantee: all cores see a single order of writes to each individual line. It says nothing about the order of writes to different lines, which is the memory model's job, and this distinction is where most concurrency confusion lives. A line ping-ponging between M on two cores costs a coherence transaction per write, and cross-core transfer latency on one socket is commonly in the tens of nanoseconds, versus about a nanosecond for an L1 hit. Keep written data private to one core: the single-writer principle behind the LMAX Disruptor. When sharing is unavoidable, share read-mostly data, since any number of cores may hold a line in S simultaneously at no ongoing cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: Core 0 reads line X (no other copy), then writes it. Core 1 then reads X, then writes it. List the state transitions for both cores and every coherence message, for {n} repetitions of that cycle.
L4.answer: Core 0: I to E on the read miss (no message beyond the fill), E to M on the write with no bus traffic. Core 1's read forces core 0 to supply the line and drop to S (or O), core 1 enters S. Core 1's write sends a read-for-ownership, core 0 goes to I, core 1 goes to M. Each repetition costs one data transfer plus one invalidation, so n repetitions cost n round trips of cross-core latency.
L4.explanation: The E state saves the first write entirely; everything after that is ping-pong. This trace is exactly what false sharing produces, except that with false sharing the two cores are not even touching the same variable.

L4.prompt_tpl: A counter is incremented {n} times per second by 8 threads. Which design has the lowest coherence cost?
options: One shared atomic counter, since atomics are implemented in hardware
Eight per-thread counters on separate cache lines, summed on read
One shared counter guarded by a mutex, since the mutex serialises access
L4.answer: Eight per-thread counters on separate cache lines, summed on read
L4.explanation: Both shared designs force the line to migrate between cores on every increment; the mutex adds its own contended line on top. Per-thread counters on distinct lines make every increment an L1 hit, and the read side pays a single fan-in that is usually far rarer than the writes.

L0.body:
# MOESI (AMD): adds  O = Owned  -- dirty AND shared.
#   The owner supplies data to readers WITHOUT writing back to memory.
#   MESI would have to write back to memory to move M -> S.
#
# MESIF (Intel): adds  F = Forward -- one designated sharer answers reads.
#   Without F, every core holding S could respond: redundant traffic.
#
# SNOOPING   : broadcast to all caches. O(n) traffic. Fine to ~8-16 cores.
# DIRECTORY  : a directory tracks which cores hold each line; point-to-point
#              messages only. Required at high core counts and across sockets.
L0.cloze:
MOESI's {{c1::Owned}} state lets a dirty line be shared without a {{c2::writeback}} to memory.
MESIF's {{c3::Forward}} state designates one sharer to {{c4::respond}} to read requests.
Beyond roughly 16 cores, {{c5::snooping}} is replaced by {{c6::directory}} coherence.

concepts.L1: Extensions that remove specific inefficiencies in MESI. Owned allows a dirty line to be shared with the owner responsible for supplying it. Forward nominates a single responder among sharers. Directory protocols replace broadcast with point-to-point messages tracked by a directory.
concepts.L2: The reason to know these is scaling, not trivia. Snooping is broadcast, so its traffic grows with core count and it stops being viable somewhere in the low tens of cores. Every large multi-socket and every GPU-scale coherent fabric is directory-based, and that changes the latency you should expect for a shared line.
concepts.L3: MESI's inefficiency: to move a Modified line into Shared it must be written back to memory, because Shared means clean. MOESI's Owned state means dirty and shared, with the owner obliged to supply data and eventually write back, so the memory write is deferred or avoided. MESIF attacks a different waste: with plain MESI several cores in Shared could all answer a read request, so Intel designates exactly one as Forward. Directory coherence is the structural change: instead of asking every cache, a directory entry per line records the sharer set, and only those caches are messaged. Measure them on your own topology.

L4.prompt_tpl: Under plain MESI, core 0 holds line X Modified and core 1 issues {n} reads of X interleaved with core 0 writing it. Explain what MOESI's Owned state removes from this traffic.
L4.answer: Under MESI, each transition from Modified to Shared requires writing the line back to memory, because Shared must be clean. Under MOESI the line becomes Owned: it stays dirty, core 0 supplies the data directly to core 1, and no memory write happens until the line is finally evicted. That removes one memory write per read-after-write transition.
L4.explanation: The win is proportional to how often dirty lines are read by other cores, which is exactly the producer-consumer pattern. It does not remove the cross-core transfer, so the latency cost of sharing remains.

L4.prompt_tpl: A snooping protocol broadcasts to all {c} caches on a miss. Give the asymptotic message count per miss for snooping and for a directory protocol with an average sharer count of {s}, and say where the crossover matters.
L4.answer: Snooping is order c messages per miss regardless of sharing; directory is order s plus a constant for the directory lookup. Since typical sharer counts are small, directory traffic is roughly independent of core count while snooping grows linearly, which is why every large or multi-socket system is directory-based. The cost is an extra hop of latency to consult the directory.
L4.explanation: This is a bandwidth-versus-latency trade at the fabric level: directories cut traffic at the price of an indirection. It is the same argument that decides NUMA remote access costs and why those are measured, not assumed.

L0.cloze:
Pad shared-but-independent counters to {{c1::64}} bytes, or {{c2::128}} where an adjacent-line prefetcher pairs lines.
Query the real line size with `{{c3::getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE}}`.

concepts.L1: Two threads writing different variables that happen to occupy the same cache line force the line to migrate between cores on every write, exactly as if they shared the variable. The compiler and the source give no hint that this is happening.
concepts.L2: Do the arithmetic before padding everything. The cost is one cross-core coherence transfer per write, typically tens of nanoseconds versus roughly a nanosecond for an L1 hit, so the slowdown is bounded by that ratio and only bites on genuinely hot counters. Padding cold structures wastes cache for nothing.
concepts.L3: Take eight threads incrementing eight adjacent 8-byte counters at $10^{8}$ increments each. Padded, every increment is an L1 hit at roughly one cycle, so the work is about $10^{8}$ cycles per thread, all in parallel. Unpadded, every increment needs exclusive ownership of the one shared line, so the increments serialise and each pays a cross-core transfer. Using a conservative 60 cycles per transfer, total time is about $8 \times 10^{8} \times 60$ cycles of serialised work. The three diagnostic signals are: the slowdown grows with thread count, it vanishes when you add padding, and hardware counters show high coherence or HITM events rather than misses to DRAM.

L4.prompt_tpl: {t} threads each perform {n} increments of separate 8-byte counters packed into one 64-byte line. An L1 hit costs 1 cycle; a cross-core coherence transfer costs {k} cycles and serialises the increments. Estimate the padded and unpadded times in cycles and the ratio. Answer with the ratio of unpadded to padded time.
L4.answer: Padded: about $n$ cycles wall clock, since threads run in parallel on their own lines. Unpadded: about $t \cdot n \cdot k$ cycles, since every increment serialises on the shared line. Ratio is about $t \cdot k$. For $t=8, k=60$: about 480x in this idealised model.
L4.explanation: The model overstates the real ratio because store buffers and coalescing recover some of it; measured results are usually 10x to 100x. Use the model to decide whether to investigate, then measure. The key structural point is that the penalty scales with thread count, so it gets worse exactly as you add hardware.

L4.prompt_tpl: A metrics library allocates `uint64_t counters[{n}]` and hands out one index per thread. Throughput drops as thread count rises. Name the defect, the fix, and the counter that confirms it.
L4.answer: False sharing: eight counters per 64-byte line, so threads on different cores contend for the same line. Fix: pad each counter to a full line with alignas(64), or 128 bytes where adjacent-line prefetching pairs lines. Confirm with HITM or cross-core coherence counters (on Linux, perf c2c is purpose-built for this) rather than with plain cache-miss counts.
L4.explanation: perf c2c exists precisely for this bug and reports the offending cache line and the source lines that touch it. Plain miss counters will not show it clearly because the line is in cache, just in the wrong core's cache.

concepts.L1: L1 ~4 cycles (~1ns), L2 ~12 cycles, L3 ~40 cycles (~15ns), DRAM ~200-300 cycles (~80ns), NVMe ~50-100μs, network round trip within a datacenter ~0.5ms, cross-continent ~150ms.

Recent x86 parts show L1 load-use around 4 to 5 cycles, L2 in the low teens, L3 from about 30 to well over 50 cycles and idle DRAM around 70 to 100 ns rising sharply under load. The ratio is what generalises: one DRAM miss costs what several hundred arithmetic operations cost, so a data layout change that removes misses beats an algorithmic change that removes arithmetic almost every time. Get the curve for your own machine with a pointer-chase over a growing working set; the plateaus name your cache sizes and the step heights name your latencies.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop performs {ops} arithmetic operations per element at IPC {ipc} on a {ghz} GHz core, and misses to DRAM once per element at {ns} ns. L4.answer: compute time $= ops/(ipc \cdot ghz)$ ns; memory fraction $= ns/(ns + \text{compute})$. For $ops=10$, $ipc=4$, $ghz=3.0$: compute $=0.83$ ns, memory fraction $=99$ percent. Compute dominates only above roughly $ns \cdot ipc \cdot ghz$ operations, here about 960.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run a pointer-chase benchmark over working sets from {lo} KB to {hi} MB and plot latency against size. Describe the shape and what each feature tells you.
