The step positions read off L1, L2 and L3 sizes; a further step near the TLB reach appears if the stride exceeds a page, since page walks are then added on top.
L4.explanation: Randomising the chase order defeats the prefetcher, which is required for the plateaus to show true latency. A sequential chase measures prefetched bandwidth instead and gives a flat, misleadingly fast line.

concepts.L3: Bandwidth efficiency is useful bytes divided by bytes transferred, and it is computable from the layout alone. For a 200-byte struct where you touch a 4-byte field, each element you want sits in a different line, so you move 64 bytes to use 4: about 6 percent. Switch to struct of arrays and the same loop moves 64 bytes to use 64. The gain is not the 16x the ratio suggests, because you were probably not bandwidth-saturated to begin with, but it is often several times. This also interacts with the prefetcher: sequential access over a dense array is detected and prefetched, while striding through structs at 200 bytes may or may not be, depending on the stride and the page boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: You convert a {sz}-byte struct array to struct-of-arrays and see only a {g}x speedup rather than the 16x the traffic ratio predicts. What is the most likely explanation?

Struct-of-arrays has worse temporal locality

L4.explanation: Negative scaling with thread count is the fingerprint. If adding cores makes a workload slower and the profile shows no lock contention, look for a shared line before looking anywhere else.

concepts.L2: First-touch means the thread that first writes a page determines its socket — so initializing a large array from one thread and processing it from many gives you all-remote access. Parallel initialization is the fix, and it's counterintuitive.

L4.answer: Replicate it per node if memory allows, otherwise interleave pages across nodes
L4.explanation: Read-only data is the one case where replication is safe and removes remote access entirely. Where the table is too large to duplicate, interleaving at least balances the remote traffic and the bandwidth load instead of concentrating it on one node's controller.

concepts.L1: Hardware prefetchers detect sequential and strided patterns. Software prefetch intrinsics for patterns they can't detect, like pointer chasing with a known lookahead.
concepts.L2: Hardware prefetchers don't cross page boundaries, which is another argument for huge pages in streaming workloads.
concepts.L3: The page-boundary limit follows from the design: a hardware prefetcher works on physical addresses and cannot know which physical page follows the current one, so streams restart at every 4 KiB boundary. With 64-byte lines that is a restart every 64 lines, and the first accesses after each boundary are unprefetched. Software prefetch fills a different gap: patterns the hardware cannot recognise, above all indexed and pointer-based access where the address depends on data. It requires a lookahead distance you must tune empirically, and it is easy to make things worse by issuing prefetches that evict live lines or that consume load-port bandwidth for nothing.

L4.explanation: Two distinct benefits share one knob, which is why huge-page results are often larger than a TLB-only model predicts. It also means huge pages can help streaming workloads whose TLB counters look perfectly healthy.

concepts.L2: This is the single most useful mental model for GPU and CPU optimization. Most deep learning kernels — elementwise ops, normalization, attention before FlashAttention — are memory bound, which is why fusion delivers such large wins.

concepts.t: DRAM organisation: channel, rank, bank, row

L0.body:
sudo dmidecode -t memory | grep -E 'Speed|Type|Size'
sudo lshw -short -C memory

#  CPU
#   └─ memory controller
#       └─ CHANNEL      (independent bus; 2-12 per socket on servers)
#           └─ DIMM / RANK  (a set of chips answering together, 64 data bits)
#               └─ BANK GROUP → BANK  (independent state machines, 16-32 banks)
#                   └─ ROW  (8-16 KiB; ONE row per bank may be OPEN)
#                       └─ COLUMN  (the burst you actually read: 64 B)
L0.cloze:
The hierarchy is channel, {{c1::rank}}, bank group, {{c2::bank}}, row, column.
Each bank may have exactly {{c3::one}} row open at a time, held in its {{c4::row buffer}}.

concepts.L1: DRAM is not a flat array. An address is decoded into channel, rank, bank and then row and column. Banks are independent state machines, so several can be busy at once, which is where memory-level parallelism at the device comes from.
concepts.L2: Banks, not channels, are what make random access survivable. A single channel with 32 banks can have 32 row activations in flight; the sequential-versus-random gap you measure is mostly about whether your addresses spread across banks or pile into one.
concepts.L3: Reading a byte means: select the bank, activate its row (copying an entire 8 to 16 KiB row into the sense amplifiers, which is destructive and must later be restored), then read the column burst. The row buffer is therefore a cache with exactly one entry per bank, and the access classes are: row hit, where the wanted row is already open and only the column read is paid; row miss on an idle bank, where an activate is added; and row conflict, where a different row is open and must first be precharged. Address interleaving policy decides which of these you get. A stride that lands every access on one bank is the device-level twin of cache conflict misses.

L4.prompt_tpl: A benchmark strides through memory by exactly {stride} KiB and is far slower than a sequential scan of the same total bytes, with no change in TLB or cache miss counts. Explain the mechanism at the DRAM level.
L4.answer: The stride is a multiple of the controller's bank and channel interleaving period, so every access maps to the same bank and often to a different row within it. Each access is then a row conflict requiring precharge plus activate plus column read, and they serialise on one bank instead of spreading across the tens of banks a sequential scan uses.
L4.explanation: This is why power-of-two strides are hazardous at every level: they alias in the cache index bits and in the DRAM address decode. The fix is the same in both cases, which is to perturb the stride by one line or one page.

L4.prompt_tpl: A channel has {b} banks and a row is {r} KiB. How many distinct rows can be open simultaneously on that channel, and how many bytes of row-buffer capacity does that represent? Answer with the row-buffer capacity in KiB.
L4.answer: One row per bank, so $b$ rows open and $b \cdot r$ KiB of row-buffer capacity. For 32 banks and 8 KiB rows: 32 rows and 256 KiB.
L4.explanation: That capacity is comparable to an L2 cache, which is why sequential and moderately-strided access patterns get a large hit rate in row buffers and why they are so much cheaper than truly random access. It is a real cache and worth reasoning about as one.

# row HIT      = tCL

# row CONFLICT = tRP + tRCD + tCL        (a different row was open)

concepts.L2: This is the whole reason latency and bandwidth diverged. DDR5 doubles transfer rate over DDR4 and delivers the first byte at the same time. Anything you write that is latency-bound gets no faster when you buy faster memory; only bandwidth-bound code does.
concepts.L3: Convert two data points and the pattern is unmistakable. DDR4-3200 CL22 runs a 1600 MHz memory clock, so tCL is $22/1600 \times 10^{6}$ seconds, about 13.75 ns. DDR5-6400 CL46 runs 3200 MHz, so tCL is about 14.4 ns. Identical latency, double the peak transfer rate. The physics explains it: sensing a row is an analogue operation on a tiny capacitor and does not scale with bus frequency. The row-conflict-to-row-hit ratio of roughly 3x means access order matters enormously; sorting accesses by address, or batching them so a row is drained before moving on, converts conflicts into hits.

# Little's law applied to the memory system:
#     concurrency (bytes in flight) = bandwidth x latency
#
# One core, 10 line-fill buffers, 64-byte lines, 80 ns latency:
#     bytes in flight = 10 * 64 = 640 B
#     max bandwidth   = 640 B / 80 ns = 8 GB/s
#
# A server with 100+ GB/s of memory bandwidth therefore needs
#     100 / 8 = ~13 cores  running memory-bound code to saturate it.
# A SINGLE core cannot saturate a modern memory system. This is why
# single-threaded STREAM numbers look disappointing and are not a defect.
L0.cloze:
Little's law: bytes in flight = {{c1::bandwidth}} x {{c2::latency}}.
One core with 10 fill buffers at 80 ns is capped near {{c3::8}} GB/s, so saturating a 100 GB/s system needs roughly {{c4::13}} cores.

concepts.L1: Bandwidth and latency are linked by concurrency. To sustain $B$ bytes per second at latency $L$ you must keep $B \cdot L$ bytes outstanding at all times. Since a core has a small fixed number of outstanding-miss slots, its achievable bandwidth is capped independently of the memory system's peak.
concepts.L2: Peak bandwidth is a property of the whole socket and is unreachable from one thread. People benchmark memcpy single-threaded, get a fraction of the specification, and conclude the hardware underperforms. The limit is the fill buffers, and the fix is more cores or more independent streams per core.
concepts.L3: Take a core with 10 outstanding line-fill buffers, 64-byte lines and 80 ns of DRAM latency. The most it can have in flight is 640 bytes, and it drains and refills them every 80 ns, so its ceiling is 8 GB/s. Add a second independent stream inside the same thread and nothing changes, because the limit is buffers, not streams. Add cores and it scales roughly linearly until the channels saturate. This also explains why reducing latency raises single-core bandwidth: at 60 ns the same 640 bytes give 10.7 GB/s. Fill buffer counts are generation-specific and often around 10 to 16 on x86 cores, so measure your own ceiling with a multi-stream read benchmark rather than trusting the number.

L4.prompt_tpl: A core has {mshr} outstanding-miss slots of {line} bytes and DRAM latency is {lat} ns. Give the single-core bandwidth ceiling, and the number of such cores needed to saturate {sys} GB/s. Answer with the single-core bandwidth ceiling in GB/s.
L4.answer: ceiling $= mshr \cdot line/lat$; cores $= \lceil sys/\text{ceiling} \rceil$. For 12 slots, 64 B, 80 ns: $768/80\times10^{-9} = 9.6$ GB/s, so about 11 cores for 100 GB/s and 42 for 400 GB/s.
L4.explanation: The result explains a lot of benchmarking confusion: STREAM must be run with enough threads to reach the platform number, and a service pinned to a few cores can be bandwidth-limited long before the socket is. It also shows why lower latency raises single-core bandwidth even though bandwidth and latency are nominally independent.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using Little's law, explain why a dependent pointer chase over {n} nodes achieves a bandwidth of roughly one cache line per memory latency regardless of how many fill buffers the core has.
L4.answer: Each node's address is only known once the previous node's line arrives, so concurrency is pinned at one outstanding miss. By Little's law bandwidth equals concurrency divided by latency, which is 64 bytes per 80 ns, about 0.8 GB/s. The remaining fill buffers cannot be used because there is no independent address to issue.
L4.explanation: This is the quantitative statement of why pointer chasing is slow: not the indirection itself but the loss of memory-level parallelism. Any restructuring that lets several independent chases run at once, such as processing multiple queries in an interleaved batch, recovers the concurrency and most of the bandwidth.

concepts.t: Memory-level parallelism and the fill buffers

L0.cloze:
MLP is the number of {{c1::independent}} misses in flight.
Interleaving four independent traversals raises MLP from 1 to {{c2::4}} at identical instruction count.
The ceiling is the core's supply of {{c3::fill buffers}}.

concepts.L1: Memory-level parallelism is how many cache misses a core can have outstanding at once. Independent misses overlap and cost roughly one latency in total; dependent misses serialise and cost one latency each. This single distinction explains most memory-bound performance differences.
concepts.L2: Counting misses is not counting cost. Two programs with identical miss counts can differ by an order of magnitude purely in how many of those misses overlap, and no cache-miss counter distinguishes them. The right question is never how many misses but how many are independent.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is the set of miss-status holding registers, called line fill buffers on Intel parts, roughly 10 to 16 per core depending on generation. When a miss issues and a buffer is free it is allocated and execution continues; the core stalls only when it needs the data or runs out of buffers. So a batch of independent misses costs about one latency plus a small ramp, while a dependent chain costs one latency per link. The practical technique is to create independent streams: process several queries at once, split a tree traversal into multiple concurrent probes. Measure MLP indirectly by comparing achieved bandwidth against the Little's law ceiling.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop performs {m} cache misses at {lat} ns each. Give the total memory time when the misses are fully dependent and when they are independent with MLP capped at {mlp}. Answer with the total memory time in nanoseconds when the misses are independent.
L4.answer: Dependent: $m \cdot lat$. Independent: about $m \cdot lat / mlp$. For $m=10^{6}$, $lat=80$ ns, $mlp=10$: 80 ms versus 8 ms.
L4.explanation: Same miss count, tenfold difference in time. This is why a profiler reporting cache misses is only half a diagnosis, and why the fix for memory-bound code is often to restructure for concurrency rather than to reduce the miss count at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hash join probes {n} keys, each a single dependent random access. Which change gives the largest speedup, assuming the table does not fit in cache?
options: Switch to a cache-friendlier hash function to reduce collisions
Interleave several probes in flight, or software-prefetch the bucket a fixed lookahead ahead, to raise memory-level parallelism
Increase the table size so the load factor drops
L4.answer: Interleave several probes in flight, or software-prefetch the bucket a fixed lookahead ahead, to raise memory-level parallelism
L4.explanation: The miss count per probe is already close to one; the problem is that they are serialised. Raising MLP converts n serial latencies into about n/MLP. A larger table makes locality worse, and hash quality changes collisions rather than concurrency.

concepts.t: The page walk and what a TLB miss costs

L0.body:
# x86-64, 4-level paging (48-bit VA). 5-level with LA57 (57-bit VA).
#   CR3 -> PML4E -> PDPTE -> PDE -> PTE -> physical frame
#            ^ each level is a MEMORY access that can itself miss
#
# Page-walk caches hold the upper levels, so a typical walk is 1-2 accesses.
# A cold walk with every level missing costs up to 4 dependent DRAM accesses:
#   4 x ~80 ns = ~320 ns for ONE translation.
#
perf stat -e dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,dtlb_load_misses.walk_completed ./a.out
#   walk_active / cycles = fraction of time spent walking page tables
L0.cloze:
x86-64 uses {{c1::4}} levels of page tables (5 with LA57), so a cold walk is up to {{c2::4}} dependent memory accesses.
{{c3::Page-walk caches}} usually satisfy the upper levels.
Measure with `{{c4::walk_active}}` as a fraction of cycles.

concepts.L1: A TLB miss is resolved in hardware by walking the page tables. Each level is a memory access, and the accesses are dependent, so they cannot overlap. Page-walk caches hold recently used upper levels and reduce the typical walk to one or two accesses.
concepts.L2: The walk accesses go through the normal data caches, so a hot page table is cheap and a cold one is not. That means TLB cost is not a fixed constant: the same miss rate can cost ten times more in a large sparse structure than in a compact one, because the page tables themselves fall out of cache.
concepts.L3: Four levels, each a dependent load, is the worst case: about 320 ns at 80 ns per access, which is four times the cost of the data miss it was trying to translate. In practice page-walk caches keep PML4 and PDPT entries close, so a typical walk touches one or two levels and lands in L2 or L3. The measurement that matters is `walk_active` cycles as a fraction of total cycles, since it captures both frequency and cost. Two structural mitigations exist and they are different: huge pages remove a level from the walk and multiply TLB reach, while improving locality reduces how many distinct pages are touched at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: A workload takes {miss} TLB misses per second. Each walk averages {acc} dependent memory accesses at {lat} ns. On a {ghz} GHz core, what fraction of one core's time is page walking? Answer with the fraction of one core's time spent page walking.
L4.answer: time per walk $= acc \cdot lat$ ns; fraction $= miss \cdot acc \cdot lat \times 10^{-9}$. For $10^{7}$ misses, 1.5 accesses, 80 ns: $1.2 \times 10^{-3}$ seconds per second, i.e. 0.12 percent. At $5\times10^{7}$ misses and 4 accesses: 20 percent.
L4.explanation: The point is the range. TLB cost is negligible or dominant depending on both the miss rate and how cached the page tables are, so the same counter value means different things in different programs. Always convert to a fraction of cycles with walk_active rather than judging raw miss counts.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why 2 MiB pages reduce page-walk cost in two independent ways, and why {n} GiB pages are not simply strictly better.
L4.answer: First, a 2 MiB mapping terminates the walk one level early, so a walk is shorter. Second, each TLB entry covers 512 times more memory, so far fewer walks happen at all. 1 GiB pages extend both effects but require contiguous physical memory reserved up front, waste memory through internal fragmentation, make allocation and page-fault latency much lumpier, and are unsuitable for sparse or dynamically-sized regions.
L4.explanation: Bigger pages are a locality-versus-fragmentation trade, not a free win. Databases commonly use 2 MiB pages for the buffer pool and 4 KiB elsewhere for exactly this reason, and 1 GiB pages are mostly reserved for fixed-size preallocated arenas.

concepts.t: Huge pages: when they help and when they hurt

L0.body:
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
always [madvise] never
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag
[always] defer defer+madvise madvise never

grep -E 'AnonHugePages|HugePages_' /proc/meminfo
grep -E 'thp_fault_alloc|thp_collapse_alloc' /proc/vmstat

# Explicit, reserved 1 GiB pages (boot parameter, not runtime):
#   default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=64
# Redis, MongoDB and several JVM tuning guides recommend THP=never
# because compaction stalls show up directly in tail latency.
L0.cloze:
THP policy is `always`, `{{c1::madvise}}` or `never`; the {{c2::defrag}} knob controls whether allocation may stall to compact memory.
Latency-sensitive services often set THP to {{c3::never}} because compaction stalls hit the {{c4::tail}}.

concepts.L1: Huge pages trade allocation flexibility for translation efficiency. Transparent huge pages let the kernel promote 4 KiB pages to 2 MiB automatically; explicit hugetlbfs pages must be reserved. Both raise TLB reach by 512x and extend hardware prefetch streams.
concepts.L2: The failure mode is a latency one, not a throughput one. Synchronous compaction to find a contiguous 2 MiB region can stall an allocating thread for milliseconds, which is invisible in throughput benchmarks and devastating in p99. That is why several latency-sensitive databases ship with instructions to disable THP.
concepts.L3: Decide from your own measurements in two steps. First, compute TLB reach and compare with the working set; if the working set fits the 4 KiB reach, huge pages buy nothing and should not be enabled. Second, check whether the workload is streaming, since prefetch streams restart at page boundaries and huge pages help there even when TLB reach is adequate. The middle setting, `madvise`, is usually the right default: the process asks for huge pages where it wants them via `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` and nothing else is promoted behind your back. Confirm the effect with `walk_active` cycles before and after, and check `/proc/vmstat` for compaction stall counters when you see tail regressions.

L4.prompt_tpl: A latency-critical service with a {gb} GiB heap sees p50 improve and p99 worsen after enabling THP=always. What is happening and what setting do you choose?
L4.answer: p50 improves because TLB reach rose and typical accesses translate faster. p99 worsens because some allocations trigger synchronous compaction to assemble a contiguous 2 MiB region, stalling that thread for milliseconds. Choose THP=madvise with defrag set to defer or madvise, and request huge pages explicitly for the long-lived heap region, or preallocate with hugetlbfs.
L4.explanation: This is the standard resolution: keep the translation benefit for the region you control and remove the kernel's freedom to stall arbitrary allocations. Measure both percentiles before and after, since a mean-only benchmark will report an improvement either way.

L4.prompt_tpl: A second-level TLB has {e} entries and the hot working set is {ws} MiB accessed randomly. Compute reach with 4 KiB and 2 MiB pages, and predict whether huge pages will help. Answer with the 4 KiB-page reach in MiB.
L4.answer: Reach is $e \cdot 4$ KiB and $e \cdot 2$ MiB. For $e=1536$: 6 MiB and 3072 MiB. A 4 MiB working set already fits the small-page reach, so huge pages will not help translation. A 64 MiB or 2048 MiB set exceeds 6 MiB and fits 3072 MiB, so huge pages should substantially cut walks.
L4.explanation: Doing this arithmetic first avoids the most common mistake, which is enabling huge pages on a workload whose translations were never the bottleneck and then attributing unrelated noise to the change.

concepts.t: Vector width, lanes and the vector register file

L0.cloze:
AVX-512 vectors hold {{c1::16}} floats; NEON is fixed at {{c2::128}} bits.
SVE and RVV are {{c3::vector-length agnostic}}: the same binary runs at any implemented width, using a {{c4::predicate}} instead of a remainder loop.

concepts.L1: A vector register holds several elements processed as lanes by one instruction. Width is fixed per instruction set on x86 and NEON, and runtime-variable on SVE and RVV, where a predicate register selects which lanes are active.
concepts.L2: Doubling the width rarely doubles throughput. Loads and stores, shuffles and the loop's dependence structure often bind first, and on many parts the wide units are fewer than the narrow ones, so 512-bit code issues at half the rate per instruction. Expect a fraction of the paper factor.
concepts.L3: Think in lanes, not in bits. A 512-bit register holds 16 fp32 lanes, so one FMA does 32 FLOPs and, with two FMA units, a core can retire 64 FLOPs per cycle in fp32. That is the number in the roofline peak. What stops you reaching it is usually elsewhere: two loads per cycle at 64 bytes each is 128 bytes per cycle of load bandwidth, which for a dot product means you are load bound before you are FMA bound. Register count matters too: 32 zmm registers versus 16 ymm is often worth more than the width itself for blocked kernels, because it permits larger register tiles.

L4.prompt_tpl: A core has {u} FMA units of {w} bits each at {ghz} GHz. Give peak fp32 FLOP/s per core, and the load bandwidth in bytes per cycle needed to feed a dot product at that rate. Answer with the peak fp32 GFLOP/s per core.
L4.answer: lanes $= w/32$; FLOPs per cycle $= 2 \cdot u \cdot lanes$; peak $= $ that $\times ghz \times 10^{9}$. For $u=2$, $w=512$, $ghz=3.0$: 64 FLOP/cycle, 192 GFLOP/s. A dot product needs 2 loads per FMA, so $2 \cdot u \cdot w/8 = 128$ bytes per cycle, which exceeds the 2 loads per cycle most cores provide at 64 bytes each.
L4.explanation: The arithmetic shows the dot product is load-port bound, not FMA bound, on this configuration. That is why real GEMM kernels block for register reuse: each loaded value must feed many FMAs before it is evicted from a register.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why an SVE loop over {n} elements needs no remainder loop, and what that removes from the generated code.
L4.answer: svwhilelt produces a predicate that is all-true for full iterations and partially true for the final one, so the same loop body handles the tail with inactive lanes masked off. That removes the scalar epilogue, the branch that selects it, and the code-size and branch-prediction cost of both, and it makes the binary independent of the implementation's vector length.
L4.explanation: AVX-512 has the same masking capability and can be used the same way, so the technique is not exclusive to SVE. The difference is that SVE makes it the default idiom and additionally makes the width a runtime property rather than a compile-time one.

turbostat --quiet --show Core,Bzy_MHz,PkgWatt,PkgTmp -- ./a.out
#   watch Bzy_MHz DROP when the 512-bit loop starts, and stay down for
#   roughly 680 microseconds after the last wide instruction.

# Skylake-SP / Cascade Lake license levels (Travis Downs, W-2104 measurements):
#   L0 non-AVX turbo      3.2 GHz
#   L1 AVX / AVX2 turbo   2.8 GHz
#   L2 AVX-512 turbo      2.4 GHz
#
# ICE LAKE SERVER AND LATER: much smaller. AMD Zen 4/5: no license levels.
# GENERATION-DEPENDENT. MEASURE WITH turbostat ON YOUR PART.

On Skylake-SP the three license levels are {{c1::L0}}, {{c2::L1}} and {{c3::L2}}, with L2 the AVX-512 turbo.
After the last wide instruction the CPU stays down-clocked for about {{c4::680}} microseconds.
Measure with `{{c5::turbostat}}` because the effect is generation-dependent.

concepts.L1: Wide vector instructions draw more current, so some parts drop core frequency to stay inside voltage and thermal limits. On Skylake-SP and Cascade Lake this was formalised as license levels with distinct turbo ceilings for scalar, 256-bit and 512-bit code.
concepts.L2: The cost is not confined to the vectorised loop. The frequency stays reduced for hundreds of microseconds afterwards, so a brief AVX-512 memcpy inside a request handler slows down the unrelated scalar code that follows it. That is why a local speedup can be a global regression.
concepts.L3: Downs measured the mechanism on a W-2104: a transition begins with a throttle period of roughly 8 to 20 microseconds during which instructions issue at about a quarter rate, and the higher licence persists until roughly 680 microseconds have passed with no wide instruction. Sparse use is the worst case: you pay the transition repeatedly and never amortise it, so either use AVX-512 in long sustained loops or not at all. These numbers age: Ice Lake server and later Intel parts reduced the penalty substantially, and AMD's Zen 4 and Zen 5 have no equivalent license-level scheme. Reproduce it with `turbostat` while your kernel runs, and compare end-to-end program time, not loop time.

L4.prompt_tpl: A request handler runs a {us} microsecond AVX-512 loop that is {sp}x faster than the scalar version, then {rest} microseconds of scalar work. The wide loop drops frequency from {f0} to {f2} GHz and the reduced frequency persists through the scalar section. Does the change help?
L4.answer: Compute saved time in the loop against added time in the tail. The scalar tail now runs at $f2/f0 = 0.75$ of its speed, costing $rest \cdot (f0/f2 - 1) = rest \cdot 0.333$ extra microseconds. For $rest=600$ that is 200 microseconds of penalty against a loop saving of at most $us \cdot (1 - 1/sp)$, which for $us=20, sp=4$ is 15 microseconds. Net: a large regression.
L4.explanation: The asymmetry is the lesson: the win is bounded by the length of the vector loop and the loss is proportional to everything that runs in the next 680 microseconds. Always measure whole-request time, and remember that on Ice Lake server and later, or on Zen 4 and 5, this arithmetic can come out completely differently.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your microbenchmark shows an AVX-512 kernel is {sp}x faster than AVX2, but the full service gets slower. Which measurement settles it?
options: Re-run the microbenchmark with more iterations to reduce noise
Run turbostat during the full service and compare busy MHz and end-to-end latency percentiles with and without the kernel
Check the disassembly to confirm the compiler used zmm registers
L4.answer: Run turbostat during the full service and compare busy MHz and end-to-end latency percentiles with and without the kernel
L4.explanation: A microbenchmark of the kernel alone runs it continuously, so it pays the transition once and amortises it. The service pays it repeatedly and exports the frequency drop to unrelated code. Only a whole-system measurement with frequency instrumentation can show that.

concepts.t: Gather and scatter: the cost of non-contiguity

L0.cloze:
A gather is one {{c1::instruction}} but {{c2::8}} independent memory accesses for a 256-bit fp32 gather.
Scatter exists only in {{c3::AVX-512}}.
On many parts, plain scalar loads {{c4::tie or beat}} a gather -- check uops.info.

concepts.L1: Gather loads elements from computed addresses into one vector; scatter writes them back. They make indexed access expressible in SIMD, but the hardware still performs one access per lane, so the memory system sees no benefit at all.
concepts.L2: Gather removes instruction count, not memory traffic. If your indices are random you still take up to one cache line per lane, and the loop stays memory bound at exactly the rate it was before. Vectorising an indexed loop with gather often produces zero speedup, and people are surprised because the instruction count fell.
concepts.L3: Count the work at each level. A 256-bit fp32 gather issues 8 address computations, 8 TLB lookups and 8 cache accesses, all of which the scalar version also did. What you save is the loop overhead and the shuffle work of assembling a vector. What you do not save is anything the memory system does, and on parts where gather is microcoded it also occupies the load ports for many cycles and cannot dual-issue with other loads. The cases where gather does pay: when the indices are clustered so several lanes share a cache line, when it replaces a much longer sequence of inserts. These are empirical questions, so measure both versions rather than reasoning from the instruction count.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop gathers {lanes} fp32 elements per iteration from random positions in a {mb} MB table. Give the number of cache lines touched per iteration in the worst case, and say whether replacing scalar loads with a gather changes memory traffic. Answer with the number of cache lines touched per iteration in the worst case.
L4.answer: Up to $lanes$ distinct 64-byte lines, so 8 or 16 lines, i.e. 512 or 1024 bytes moved to use 32 or 64 useful bytes. The gather changes none of this: it issues the same accesses, so memory traffic and cache miss counts are identical.
L4.explanation: Bandwidth efficiency here is 1/16, which is the real bottleneck. The productive fixes are to change the data layout so indices are clustered, to sort or partition the indices so accesses share lines, or to raise memory-level parallelism, none of which is a SIMD change.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague vectorises an indexed sum over {n} elements with `_mm256_i32gather_ps` and reports no speedup, concluding SIMD does not work on this code. What did they measure and what should they measure instead?
L4.answer: They measured instruction count reduction and expected time reduction. The loop is memory bound: the gather performs the same 8 accesses, touches the same lines and takes the same memory time. They should measure bytes moved and achieved bandwidth against the Little's law ceiling, and then attack layout or memory-level parallelism rather than instruction count.
L4.explanation: This is the roofline argument in miniature. Below the ridge point, no instruction-level transformation helps, and the correct diagnosis is available before writing any intrinsics if you compute arithmetic intensity first.

L0.cloze:
Read the compiler's report with `{{c1::-fopt-info-vec-missed}}` before writing intrinsics.
The most common cause is {{c2::aliasing}}, fixed with `{{c3::restrict}}`.
FP reductions need permission to {{c4::reassociate}}.

concepts.L1: Compilers vectorise only when they can prove the transformation is legal. Failure is usually a proof failure rather than an inability, and the compiler will tell you which proof it could not construct if you ask for the report.
concepts.L2: The reflex to hand-write intrinsics after seeing scalar assembly is usually premature. Nine times in ten the compiler wanted to vectorise and lacked one guarantee, and one `restrict` or one pragma recovers most of the gain with none of the portability cost.
concepts.L3: Take the canonical failure: `for (i) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];` with three raw pointers. If `c` overlaps `a`, then storing to `c[i]` may change `a[i+1]`, so the iterations are not independent. `restrict` asserts non-overlap and the loop vectorises. Floating-point reductions are a different proof: vectorising a sum means summing partial vectors and combining them, which changes the order of additions, and fp addition is not associative, so the compiler needs `-ffast-math` or an explicit `#pragma omp simd reduction`. Loop-carried dependences like `a[i] = a[i-1] + x` are genuinely unvectorisable in that form and need an algorithmic change such as a prefix-sum formulation.

L4.prompt_tpl: This loop over {n} elements is not vectorised: `for (i=0;i<n;i++){{ if (a[i] < 0) break; s += a[i]*b[i]; }}`. Give the reason and a restructuring that vectorises.
L4.answer: The data-dependent exit means the trip count is unknown until the data is examined, so the compiler cannot prove it is safe to execute a whole vector's worth of iterations. Restructure as two passes: first find the index of the first negative element with a vectorisable search, then run the vectorised reduction over the known prefix. Alternatively use masked operations where the ISA supports them.
L4.explanation: Early exits, calls, and anything that can trap are the three reasons a compiler refuses to run iterations speculatively. Splitting the loop into a search and a reduction is the standard fix and usually vectorises both halves.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why `-ffast-math` is required to vectorise a `{typ}` summation, and what specifically becomes unreliable if you enable it.
L4.answer: Vectorising a sum produces several partial sums combined at the end, which reorders the additions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so the result may differ from the scalar order and the compiler needs permission to change it. Enabling -ffast-math also permits other unsafe assumptions: no NaNs or infinities, reciprocal substitution for division, and reassociation everywhere, so bitwise reproducibility and some numerical guards are lost across the whole translation unit.
L4.explanation: The targeted alternative is #pragma omp simd reduction(+:s) or the equivalent, which grants reassociation for that loop only. That is almost always the right choice, because it makes the numerical decision local and visible.

concepts.t: Masking, tails and the remainder loop

L0.cloze:
A fixed-width vector loop needs a {{c1::remainder}} loop for up to {{c2::width-1}} elements.
Masked loads and stores remove it: inactive lanes are {{c3::not written}} and do not {{c4::fault}}.

concepts.L1: When the trip count is not a multiple of the vector width, the leftover elements need handling. The traditional answer is a scalar epilogue; masked instructions handle the tail in the same vector body by disabling the surplus lanes.
concepts.L2: For short arrays the tail is the whole story. At $n = 20$ with 16-wide vectors you run one vector iteration and four scalar ones, so more than half the elements go through the slow path and the measured speedup is a fraction of the width.
concepts.L3: Quantify it. With width $w$ and trip count $n$, the vector loop covers $w \lfloor n/w \rfloor$ elements and the tail covers $n \bmod w$. At $n = 1000$ with $w = 16$ the tail is at most 15 elements, which is noise; at $n = 20$ it is 4 of 20. This is why kernels that process many short rows, such as batched small GEMMs or per-token operations in ML serving, benefit disproportionately from masking. Masking also matters for correctness: a masked load does not fault on inactive lanes, so you may read up to the array end without a guard page or an over-read, which a plain unaligned load past the end cannot promise.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vector body is {s}x faster per element than scalar at width {w}. For trip count {n}, compute the fraction of elements in the scalar tail and the overall speedup with and without masking. Answer with the unmasked time in scalar units.
L4.answer: tail $= n \bmod w$. Without masking, time $= (n - tail)/s + tail$ scalar units; with masking, time $= \lceil n/w \rceil \cdot w/s$. For $n=20$, $w=16$, $s=8$: tail 4 (20 percent), unmasked time $=16/8+4=6$ versus masked $=32/8=4$, so masking is 1.5x better.
L4.explanation: For $n=10000$ the two are within a fraction of a percent, which is why masking looks pointless in a benchmark using long arrays and matters a lot in production code full of short ones. Benchmark at the trip counts you actually run.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can a masked load safely read the last {k} elements of an array while an unaligned full-width load at the same address might fault?
L4.answer: A masked load suppresses memory access for inactive lanes entirely, so no address beyond the array end is ever touched and no fault can occur. An unaligned full-width load reads the whole vector, which may cross into an unmapped page immediately after the allocation, producing a segmentation fault that depends on where the allocator happened to place the buffer.
L4.explanation: This is a real class of intermittent crash: the over-read is harmless in almost every allocation and fatal when the buffer ends exactly at a page boundary. Masking makes the safety a property of the instruction rather than of luck.

concepts.t: Warp scheduling and latency hiding arithmetic

L0.body:
# A GPU hides latency with THREADS, not with out-of-order execution.
# Little's law again: bytes in flight = bandwidth x latency.
#
# A100 80GB, worked:
#   2039 GB/s / (108 SMs * 1.41 GHz) = ~13.4 bytes per SM per cycle
#   global load latency, measured by pointer chase: ~400-800 cycles
#   bytes needed in flight per SM = 13.4 * 500 = ~6700 B
#
#   one fully-coalesced warp load = 32 lanes * 4 B = 128 B
#   warps needed = 6700 / 128 = ~52 warps in flight per SM
#   A100 max = 64 warps per SM  ->  you need HIGH occupancy for bandwidth
L0.cloze:
GPUs hide latency with {{c1::thread-level parallelism}} rather than out-of-order execution.
Bytes in flight must equal {{c2::bandwidth}} times {{c3::latency}}.
On an A100 that works out to roughly {{c4::52}} warps per SM to saturate HBM.

concepts.L1: An SM holds many resident warps and issues from whichever ones are ready. When a warp stalls on memory, the scheduler switches to another at no cost, because every warp's registers are already allocated. Latency is hidden by having enough work resident.
concepts.L2: The occupancy you need is computable, not a rule of thumb. Little's law applied to your GPU's bandwidth and measured latency gives a specific number of concurrent requests, and that number tells you whether you are short of warps or short of independent loads inside each warp.
concepts.L3: Peak HBM bandwidth is about 2039 GB/s across 108 SMs at roughly 1.41 GHz, so each SM must absorb about 13.4 bytes per cycle. Measured global load latency on Ampere is in the region of 400 to 800 cycles, so take 500. A fully coalesced 32-lane fp32 load is 128 bytes, so you need about 52 such requests outstanding, against a hardware maximum of 64 resident warps per SM. That is why bandwidth-bound kernels usually need high occupancy. The escape hatch: a warp issuing four independent loads contributes four requests, reaching the same concurrency at a quarter of the occupancy. Measure your own latency with a pointer-chase kernel; the numbers differ by architecture and by clock state.

L4.prompt_tpl: A GPU has {bw} GB/s of memory bandwidth, {sm} SMs at {ghz} GHz, and a measured global load latency of {lat} cycles. Compute bytes needed in flight per SM and the number of fully coalesced 128-byte warp requests that implies. Answer with the number of 128-byte requests in flight per SM.
L4.answer: bytes per SM-cycle $= bw \times 10^{9}/(sm \cdot ghz \times 10^{9})$; in flight $= $ that $\times lat$; requests $= $ in flight$/128$. For 2039, 108 SMs, 1.41 GHz, 500 cycles: 13.4 B/cycle, 6700 B, about 52 requests.
L4.explanation: The result is the occupancy target for a bandwidth-bound kernel on that part. If your achieved bandwidth is far below peak and your resident warp count is far below this number, occupancy is the bottleneck; if occupancy is high and bandwidth is still low, the problem is coalescing instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel runs at {occ} percent occupancy and still achieves near-peak bandwidth. Explain how, using the concurrency requirement rather than the occupancy number.
L4.answer: Concurrency is requests in flight, not warps. If each warp issues several independent loads before consuming any of them, one warp contributes several outstanding requests. A kernel with four independent loads per thread at 25 percent occupancy has the same bytes in flight as one with a single load at 100 percent, so it saturates bandwidth equally well.
L4.explanation: This is Volkov's argument, and it generalises the occupancy heuristic into something computable. It also explains why register-heavy blocked kernels beat occupancy-maximising ones: they trade resident warps for instruction-level and memory-level parallelism per thread.

L0.cloze:
Shared memory has {{c1::32}} banks of {{c2::4}} bytes; bank = word index mod 32.
A column access into `tile[32][32]` is a {{c3::32}}-way conflict.
Padding the row to {{c4::33}} makes the bank index `(threadIdx.x + k) % 32`, which is conflict free.

concepts.L1: Shared memory is divided into 32 banks that can be accessed simultaneously. If the 32 lanes of a warp address different words in the same bank, the accesses serialise. The bank of a word is simply its index modulo 32.
concepts.L2: The one-element pad looks like a bug and is the standard fix. It costs 3 percent of shared memory and can restore 32x on a transposed access. Anyone reading the code without knowing the bank arithmetic will try to remove it.
concepts.L3: Do the modular arithmetic explicitly and the fix is obvious rather than magical. With a row length of 32 words, element $(t, k)$ is word $32t + k$, and $32t + k \equiv k \pmod{32}$: the row index drops out entirely, so every lane of the warp lands in bank $k$. Serialisation is 32-way, meaning the access takes 32 transactions rather than one. Padding the row to 33 words makes the element $33t + k$, and $33t + k \equiv t + k \pmod{32}$, which is a bijection in $t$: all 32 lanes hit distinct banks. Doubles occupy two banks per element, so the arithmetic changes; recompute rather than reusing the fp32 result. Profile with the shared memory bank conflict metrics in Nsight Compute to confirm.

L4.prompt_tpl: A __shared__ tile is declared `float tile[{r}][{c}]` and a warp reads `tile[threadIdx.x][k]` for fixed k. Give the bank index as a function of threadIdx.x and the conflict degree.
L4.answer: bank $= (c \cdot t + k) \bmod 32$. For $c=32$: $k \bmod 32$, constant in $t$, so 32-way conflict. For $c=33$: $(t + k) \bmod 32$, all distinct, conflict free. For $c=64$: $(64t + k) \bmod 32 = k \bmod 32$, again 32-way.
L4.explanation: Any row length that is a multiple of 32 collapses the bank index, so 64 is exactly as bad as 32. The rule is that the row length must be coprime with 32 for a column access, which is why odd padding is the idiom.

L4.prompt_tpl: A tiled matrix multiply uses `__shared__ float As[{n}][{n}]` and is much slower than expected, with Nsight reporting high shared memory conflicts. Give the one-line fix and explain why it works.
L4.answer: Declare it As[n][n+1]. The transposed read of the tile currently strides by n words; when n is a multiple of 32, or shares a large factor with 32, all lanes map to the same bank. Adding one word makes the stride coprime with 32, so the bank index becomes a bijection over the lane index and the access is conflict free.
L4.explanation: For n=16 the stride is 16, giving a 2-way conflict rather than 32-way, so the fix is still worth making but the gain is smaller. Computing the conflict degree rather than assuming the worst case tells you how much to expect.

concepts.L1: Occupancy is resident warps divided by the hardware maximum. Three resources cap it independently: registers per SM divided by registers per warp, shared memory per SM divided by shared memory per block, and the hardware limits on resident blocks and warps.
concepts.L2: Knowing which of the three binds is the whole diagnosis, and the compiler prints it. Reducing registers when shared memory is the limiter changes nothing; capping registers with a launch bound when registers are the limiter can double occupancy and can also cause spills that make things worse.
concepts.L3: Compute all three, take the minimum, then decide whether raising it is worth anything. On an A100 with 65536 32-bit registers per SM, a kernel using 64 registers per thread needs $64 \times 32 = 2048$ registers per warp, giving 32 resident warps against a maximum of 64: 50 percent, register limited. Using 8 KB of shared memory per block against roughly 164 KB per SM allows 20 blocks, which at 4 warps per block is 80 warps, above the cap, so shared memory is not binding here. Decide with the latency-hiding arithmetic: compute how many outstanding requests you actually need, and stop raising occupancy once you have them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel uses {regs} registers per thread and {smem} KB of shared memory per block, with {tpb} threads per block, on an SM with 65536 registers, {smsm} KB of shared memory and a 64-warp maximum. L4.answer: register warps $= \lfloor 65536/(regs \cdot 32) \rfloor$; shared blocks $= \lfloor smsm/smem \rfloor$, times $tpb/32$ warps per block; occupancy $= \min(\ldots, 64)/64$. For regs 64, smem 16, tpb 256, smsm 164: registers give 32 warps, shared gives 10 blocks times 8 warps $=80$, so 32 warps, 50 percent.
L4.explanation: Only one limiter binds at a time and the arithmetic names it. Note the real hardware also rounds register allocation to a granularity, so the compiler's occupancy calculator can differ slightly from this model; use it to confirm.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your kernel is register limited at {occ} percent occupancy and is compute bound with high arithmetic intensity. Should you add __launch_bounds__ to raise occupancy?
options: Yes: higher occupancy always hides more latency
Probably not: a compute-bound kernel needs few outstanding requests, and capping registers risks local-memory spills that add traffic
Yes, but only if shared memory usage is also reduced
L4.answer: Probably not: a compute-bound kernel needs few outstanding requests, and capping registers risks local-memory spills that add traffic
L4.explanation: Occupancy is a means to concurrency, not an end. Above the ridge point the kernel is limited by arithmetic throughput, so extra resident warps buy nothing while spills add global memory traffic that can push it below the roof. Compute the required concurrency first.

L0.body:
# A systolic array: a 2D grid of MAC cells. Weights held STATIONARY in the
# cells; activations flow in from the left, partial sums flow down.
#
#   a0 -> [w00]->[w01]->[w02] ->      each cell: psum += a * w, then PASS a
#   a1 -> [w10]->[w11]->[w12] ->      right and psum down. No register file
#   a2 -> [w20]->[w21]->[w22] ->      read per MAC. No instruction fetch.
#          |     |     |
#         psum  psum  psum
#
# TPU v1: a 256x256 array of 8-bit MACs at 700 MHz
#   = 65536 MACs * 2 ops * 0.7e9 = ~92 TOPS from ONE control stream.
L0.cloze:
A systolic array holds {{c1::weights}} stationary and streams activations across, with each cell passing operands to its {{c2::neighbour}}.
It removes the per-MAC {{c3::register file}} read and instruction fetch, which is where the energy goes.
TPU v1 was a {{c4::256x256}} array delivering about 92 TOPS.

concepts.L1: A matrix unit executes a whole tile multiply as one operation instead of a stream of scalar or vector MACs. A systolic array does it by physically laying out the multiply-accumulate cells so operands move between neighbours rather than through a register file.
concepts.L2: The gain is energy and control overhead, not raw multiplier count. A GPU could place the same number of multipliers; what it cannot avoid is fetching operands from a register file for each one. Removing that fetch is worth roughly an order of magnitude in energy per MAC.
concepts.L3: Account for one MAC on a conventional SIMD core: fetch and decode an instruction, read two source registers, do the multiply-add, write a destination register. At 45 nm the arithmetic itself is under a picojoule for fp32 while register file and control dominate. A systolic cell reuses the operand it just received by passing it to its neighbour, so one activation entering the array is used by an entire row of cells with no further fetches, and the partial sum accumulates down a column without ever being written to memory. NVIDIA's tensor cores are a different implementation of the same bargain at warp scope.

L4.prompt_tpl: A systolic array is {n}x{n} MAC cells at {ghz} GHz. Give peak operations per second counting a MAC as 2 operations, and the number of cycles of fill and drain latency before the first full result emerges. Answer with the peak operations per second.
L4.answer: peak $= n^{2} \cdot 2 \cdot ghz \times 10^{9}$ ops/s. For $n=256$, 0.7 GHz: $65536 \times 2 \times 0.7\times10^{9} = 91.8$ TOPS. Fill and drain take on the order of $2n$ cycles, here about 512, since an operand must traverse the array.
L4.explanation: The fill cost is why systolic arrays want large matrices: 512 cycles of latency is negligible amortised over a large GEMM and ruinous on a tiny one. This is the same quantisation argument as tile shape on tensor cores, expressed in hardware terms.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does a matrix unit deliver far better operations per watt than a vector unit with the same number of multipliers, at {nm} nm?
L4.answer: Because the energy of a MAC on a general core is dominated by moving operands, not by the arithmetic: instruction fetch and decode, register file reads and writes, and result forwarding. In a systolic or matrix unit an operand entering the array is reused by many cells through short local wires, and partial sums accumulate in place, so one fetch amortises over many multiplies. The multipliers cost the same in both designs; everything around them does not.
L4.explanation: This is Dally's framing: data movement is the budget. It also predicts the limits of the approach, since it only applies to operations with high reuse, which is why matrix units accelerate GEMM and convolution and do nothing for elementwise work.

# TILE quantisation: the matrix does not divide by the tile size.
#   M = 4097, tile M = 128  ->  ceil(4097/128) = 33 tiles
#   useful fraction = 4097 / (33*128) = 97%     (mild)
#   M = 129,  tile M = 128  ->  2 tiles, useful = 129/256 = 50%  (severe)
#
# WAVE quantisation: the grid does not divide by the number of SMs.
#   108 SMs, 1 resident block each, grid = 256 blocks
#   waves = ceil(256/108) = 3 ; last wave runs only 40 of 108 SMs
#   utilisation = 256 / (3*108) = 79%
#
# Both are why 'round the dimension up to a multiple of 128' is real advice.
L0.cloze:
{{c1::Tile}} quantisation wastes work inside the last tile; {{c2::wave}} quantisation wastes SMs in the last wave.
A 256-block grid on 108 SMs runs {{c3::3}} waves at {{c4::79}} percent utilisation.

concepts.L1: Two rounding losses. Tile quantisation is the waste when a matrix dimension is not a multiple of the kernel's tile size. Wave quantisation is the waste when the grid is not a multiple of the number of blocks the GPU can hold resident.
concepts.L2: These explain the discontinuous performance cliffs people report when a batch size or hidden dimension changes by one. The fix is to pick dimensions that divide cleanly, which is why model hidden sizes, head counts and vocabularies are the round numbers they are.
concepts.L3: Tile quantisation: with tile size $T$ and dimension $M$, you launch $\lceil M/T \rceil$ tiles and the useful fraction is $M/(T\lceil M/T\rceil)$. At $M=4097$ and $T=128$ that is 97 percent, barely noticeable; at $M=129$ it is 50 percent, catastrophic. Wave quantisation: with $S$ SMs each holding $b$ blocks, one wave is $Sb$ blocks and the useful fraction is $G/(Sb\lceil G/(Sb)\rceil)$ for a grid of $G$. Practical rule: round dimensions up to a multiple of 128, or of 64 at minimum, and check the resulting grid against your SM count. Then measure, because the cliff positions depend on the library's chosen tile size, which varies by version.

L4.prompt_tpl: A GEMM has M = {M} with a tile size of {T}, and launches a grid of {G} blocks on a GPU with {S} SMs holding 1 block each. Give the tile-quantisation efficiency, the wave count, and the wave-quantisation efficiency. Answer with the tile-quantisation efficiency as a fraction.
L4.answer: tiles $= \lceil M/T \rceil$, tile efficiency $= M/(T \cdot tiles)$; waves $= \lceil G/S \rceil$, wave efficiency $= G/(S \cdot waves)$. For $M=4097$, $T=128$: 33 tiles, 97 percent. For $G=256$, $S=108$: 3 waves, 79 percent. Combined about 77 percent.
L4.explanation: Multiply the two efficiencies to see total loss. Both are pure rounding, so both vanish when dimensions are chosen as multiples, which costs nothing at design time and is very expensive to retrofit into a trained model's shapes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A model's hidden dimension is changed from {a} to {b} and throughput drops sharply despite fewer FLOPs. Explain the two mechanisms that could cause it.
L4.answer: Tile quantisation: 4000 and 4090 are not multiples of the kernel's tile size, so the last tile in each dimension is partly wasted and the library may select a smaller, less efficient tile shape. Tensor core alignment: the matrix instructions require dimensions to be multiples of their tile shape, and a non-conforming size can fall back to a slower path or require padding inside the kernel. Fewer FLOPs on paper, more work in practice.
L4.explanation: This is why hidden sizes, head dimensions and vocabulary sizes in production models are multiples of 64 or 128. It is a hardware constraint that has visibly shaped model architecture, which is a good example of the silicon reaching up into the design.

L0.cloze:
A warp is {{c1::32}} threads issued together.
Divergence within a warp {{c2::serialises}} both paths; branching on {{c3::blockIdx}} instead of threadIdx keeps a warp uniform.

concepts.L1: Threads grouped into warps of 32 executing in lockstep (SIMT). Warps grouped into blocks scheduled onto streaming multiprocessors. Blocks form a grid.
concepts.L2: Warp divergence — threads in a warp taking different branches — serializes execution of both paths. A branch on threadIdx%2 halves your throughput, and this is invisible unless you know to look.
concepts.L3: SIMT means one instruction stream drives 32 lanes with a per-lane active mask. A divergent branch is executed as both paths in sequence with complementary masks, so a two-way divergence costs the sum of both sides rather than the max. Nested divergence multiplies. The practical rule is that the branch condition should be uniform across a warp: `blockIdx`-based conditions are free, `threadIdx % 2` costs double, and data-dependent conditions cost whatever fraction of warps actually diverge. Measure divergence with the branch efficiency metrics in Nsight Compute.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a warp of 32 threads, {d} lanes take path A costing {ca} cycles and the rest take path B costing {cb} cycles. Give the cycles the warp spends, and compare with the ideal if the branch were warp-uniform. Answer with the cycles the warp spends.
L4.answer: The warp executes both paths: $ca + cb$ cycles, regardless of how the lanes split. Warp-uniform would cost $ca$ or $cb$ alone. For $ca=100$, $cb=50$: 150 versus 100 or 50.
L4.explanation: The cost does not depend on the split, which surprises people: a single divergent lane costs as much as a 16-16 split. That is why sorting or partitioning work so that whole warps take the same path is the standard fix, rather than trying to balance the branch.

L4.prompt_tpl: Code that worked on Pascal by relying on warp-synchronous execution (no explicit sync inside a warp) produces wrong results on Volta and later with {n} threads per block. What changed and what is the fix?
L4.answer: Volta introduced independent thread scheduling: lanes within a warp have their own program counters and are no longer guaranteed to reconverge or to execute in lockstep at any particular point. Implicit warp-synchronous programming is therefore invalid. The fix is to use __syncwarp() and the explicit _sync variants of shuffle and vote intrinsics with an explicit mask.
L4.explanation: This is a rare case where a hardware change broke widely-used code that was always technically undefined. The _sync intrinsics were introduced precisely so the required synchronisation becomes explicit rather than implied by the scheduler's behaviour.

L0.cloze:
Registers are {{c1::per-thread}}, shared memory is {{c2::per-block}} and needs `{{c3::__syncthreads}}`.
Shared memory and {{c4::L1}} are physically the same storage on recent NVIDIA parts, split configurably.

concepts.L1: Registers (fastest, per-thread), shared memory (per-block, ~100x faster than global), L1/L2, global HBM. Shared memory is a software-managed cache and that's the point.
concepts.L2: Bank conflicts in shared memory: 32 banks, and simultaneous access to different addresses in the same bank serializes. Padding arrays by one element is the standard fix and it looks like a bug to anyone who doesn't know.
concepts.L3: The point of a software-managed scratchpad is determinism. A hardware cache decides what to keep using a policy you cannot see; shared memory keeps exactly what you put there, so a tiled algorithm can guarantee reuse rather than hope for it. The costs are explicit: you must stage data in yourself, you must synchronise with `__syncthreads` because there is no coherence, and the capacity per SM (roughly 164 KB on A100 and 228 KB on H100, configurable) directly limits how many blocks are resident. Registers remain faster still and are the real target for the innermost reuse: a good GEMM kernel keeps a register tile and touches shared memory only at the tile boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel stages a {t}x{t} fp32 tile in shared memory per block. Give the shared memory per block in bytes, and how many blocks fit in {sm} KB of shared memory per SM. Answer with the shared memory per block in bytes.
L4.answer: bytes $= t^{2} \times 4$; blocks $= \lfloor sm \times 1024 / bytes \rfloor$. For $t=32$: 4096 bytes, so 41 blocks in 164 KB, which exceeds the hardware cap on resident blocks per SM, so shared memory is not the binding limiter. For $t=64$: 16384 bytes, 10 blocks.
L4.explanation: Computing this tells you whether shared memory is your occupancy limiter before you tune anything. Note that padding a tile to t x (t+1) adds t floats per row, which is a few percent and usually well worth it against a 32-way bank conflict.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a software-managed scratchpad of {kb} KB can beat a hardware cache of the same size for a tiled matrix multiply.
L4.answer: The kernel knows the reuse pattern exactly and can guarantee that the tile stays resident for the whole inner loop. A hardware cache applies a general replacement policy and may evict the tile in favour of streaming data it has no way to know is dead, and it also fetches at line granularity whatever the access pattern. Explicit staging converts a probabilistic hit rate into a certainty.
L4.explanation: This is the general argument for scratchpads in accelerators, and the reason DSPs and TPUs use them too. The cost is that the programmer must know the pattern, which is fine for dense linear algebra and unworkable for pointer-chasing code.

L0.cloze:
A coalesced fp32 warp load moves {{c1::128}} bytes as {{c2::4}} sectors of 32 bytes.
A stride of 32 makes the same warp touch {{c3::32}} sectors, multiplying traffic.
The usual fix is {{c4::struct of arrays}}.

concepts.L1: When consecutive threads in a warp access consecutive addresses, the hardware merges them into a minimal number of transactions. Strided or random access multiplies transaction count.
concepts.L2: This is the number one determinant of naive kernel performance. A transposed access pattern can be 10-30x slower with identical arithmetic.
concepts.L3: A warp requesting 32 consecutive fp32 values covers 128 contiguous bytes, which the hardware serves as four 32-byte sectors. Introduce a stride of $S$ elements and, once $S \times 4$ exceeds the sector size, each lane needs its own sector: 32 sectors, so 1024 bytes fetched to deliver 128 useful ones, an eightfold traffic increase. Nsight Compute reports sectors per request, and comparing it against the ideal of 4 tells you immediately whether the kernel is coalesced. The remedy is nearly always structural: transpose the data, switch from array-of-structs to struct-of-arrays, or stage through shared memory so the uncoalesced access happens there instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A warp of 32 threads reads fp32 values with a stride of {S} elements. Give the number of 32-byte sectors touched and the bandwidth efficiency, against the coalesced ideal. Answer with the number of 32-byte sectors touched.
L4.answer: Bytes spanned $= 32 \cdot S \cdot 4$. Sectors $= \min(32, \lceil 32 S \cdot 4/32 \rceil)$, capped at one per lane. For $S=1$: 4 sectors, 100 percent efficient. $S=2$: 8 sectors, 50 percent. $S=8$: 32 sectors, 12.5 percent. $S=32$: 32 sectors, 12.5 percent.
L4.explanation: Efficiency floors at one sector per lane, so 32 bytes fetched per 4 useful, that is 12.5 percent. Any stride beyond 8 fp32 elements is already at the floor, which is why the AoS-to-SoA transformation matters more than the exact stride.

L4.prompt_tpl: A transposed read of a {n}x{n} matrix is 20x slower than the row-wise read with identical arithmetic. Which fix do you apply first?
options: Increase occupancy so more warps hide the latency
Stage tiles through padded shared memory so global reads stay coalesced and the transpose happens in shared memory
Use __ldg or texture loads to route the reads through a different cache
L4.answer: Stage tiles through padded shared memory so global reads stay coalesced and the transpose happens in shared memory
L4.explanation: The problem is traffic, not latency, so more warps only queue more of the same excess sectors. Moving the strided access into shared memory, where the cost is bank conflicts and a pad fixes those, converts the global access back to fully coalesced. This is the standard tiled transpose.

L0.cloze:
Nsight reports both achieved occupancy and the {{c1::limiter}} (registers, shared memory or blocks).
Issuing several {{c2::independent}} loads per thread raises concurrency without raising {{c3::occupancy}}.

concepts.L1: Ratio of active warps to maximum. Higher occupancy hides memory latency by giving the scheduler more to switch to. Limited by registers per thread and shared memory per block.
concepts.L2: Maximizing occupancy is not always right. Volkov demonstrated high performance at low occupancy by increasing instruction-level parallelism per thread. The correct target depends on whether you're latency-bound or bandwidth-bound.
concepts.L3: What the machine needs is enough outstanding memory requests to cover latency, which Little's law makes a specific number; whether those requests come from many warps each with one load, or few warps each with several independent loads, is your choice. The second option uses more registers per thread and so lowers occupancy, and for compute-heavy kernels it is often better because the register tile also increases arithmetic reuse. The decision rule: compute the required bytes in flight from bandwidth and measured latency, then check whether your kernel supplies it. If it does not, add warps or add independent loads per thread, whichever costs less.

L4.prompt_tpl: Kernel A runs at {oa} percent occupancy with 1 load in flight per thread; kernel B at {ob} percent with 4. Both are bandwidth bound on the same GPU. Which has more bytes in flight?
L4.answer: Compare occupancy times loads per thread. A at 100 percent with 1 load gives 64 warp-requests per SM; B at 25 percent with 4 loads gives 16 warps times 4, also 64. They are equal. At 75 and 30 percent, B gives 48 times 4 divided by... compute concretely: A is 48 requests, B is about 77, so B has more.
L4.explanation: Concurrency is the product, not either factor alone. This is why occupancy on its own is a poor target and why Nsight reports memory throughput alongside it: the throughput number is the one that answers the question.

L4.prompt_tpl: An SM needs {req} outstanding 128-byte requests to saturate bandwidth. Your kernel achieves {occ} percent of 64 warps with {lpt} independent loads per thread in flight. Are you saturating? Answer with the number of outstanding requests the kernel achieves.
L4.answer: requests $= 64 \cdot occ/100 \cdot lpt$. For occ 50 and lpt 2: $32 \times 2 = 64$, above 52, so saturating. For occ 25 and lpt 1: 16, far below, so not.
L4.explanation: Turning the vague occupancy question into a request count makes the fix obvious: either add warps or add independent loads. It also shows when neither will help, since once you exceed the requirement the kernel is limited by something else entirely.

wmma fragments have a fixed tile shape such as {{c1::16x16x16}} and take FP16 inputs with {{c2::FP32}} accumulation.
Hopper's {{c3::wgmma}} operates at warpgroup (128-thread) scope.
Confirm they are actually used with the `{{c4::tensor_op}}` Nsight metrics.

concepts.L1: Dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate units. Require specific data types (FP16/BF16/FP8/INT8) and specific tile shapes. An order of magnitude more throughput than CUDA cores for GEMM.
concepts.L2: They only engage if your dimensions are properly aligned — typically multiples of 8 or 16. Model dimensions that aren't multiples of 64 leave large amounts of performance unused, which is why vocab sizes and hidden dims are the numbers they are.
concepts.L3: A matrix instruction consumes a fixed tile, so a dimension that is not a multiple of that tile is padded internally or falls back to a slower path, and the library may pick a smaller tile shape with worse reuse. Combined with wave quantisation over the SM count, this is why the standard advice is to make hidden dimensions, head dimensions and vocabulary sizes multiples of 64 or 128; the effects compound. The second thing to internalise is the accumulation type: inputs are FP16, BF16, FP8 or INT8 while accumulation is wider, typically FP32, which is what keeps the numerics usable. L4.prompt_tpl: A GEMM has K = {K} and the matrix instruction consumes tiles of K = {tk}. Give the number of instruction steps, the padded K, and the fraction of arithmetic that is wasted. Answer with the number of instruction steps.
L4.answer: steps $= \lceil K/tk \rceil$; padded $= steps \cdot tk$; waste $= 1 - K/padded$. For $K=1000$, $tk=16$: 63 steps, padded 1008, 0.8 percent wasted. For $K=4097$, $tk=32$: 129 steps, padded 4128, 0.75 percent.
L4.explanation: Along a single dimension the waste is small; the damage comes from all three dimensions compounding, from the library selecting a different tile shape, and from wave quantisation on top. Compute all of them before concluding that a shape is fine.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why do tensor core paths take {t} inputs but accumulate in FP32, and what would break if accumulation were also FP16?
L4.answer: The dot product over K terms sums many products, and FP16 has about 11 bits of significand, so partial sums lose small contributions once the running total is large enough and error grows with K. FP32 accumulation keeps the sum accurate while the inputs stay narrow, which is where the bandwidth and throughput saving comes from. With FP16 accumulation, large-K GEMMs would lose accuracy in a way that shows up as training divergence rather than as a small numerical difference.
L4.explanation: This asymmetry is the whole design of mixed precision: narrow where the data volume is, wide where the error accumulates. FP8 training extends it with per-tensor scaling so the narrow format's limited range is used efficiently.

concepts.L2: This is the most important systems paper in modern ML and it's an argument about the memory hierarchy, not about attention. Standard attention is O(n²) in memory; FlashAttention is O(n), which is what made long context economically viable. Read the paper directly.

Softmax needs a maximum and a sum over the whole row, which naively forces you to see the full row before producing any output. The online formulation carries a running maximum $m$ and a running normaliser $l$, and when a new block raises the maximum it rescales the accumulated output by $\exp(m_{old} - m_{new})$. concepts.L1: The performance monitoring unit is a small set of hardware counters, typically a handful of programmable ones plus a few fixed, that increment on microarchitectural events. Sampling mode interrupts after every N events and records the instruction pointer.
concepts.L2: Two artefacts invalidate naive readings. Multiplexing: ask for more events than counters and the kernel time-slices them, scaling the results, so a rare event can be badly estimated. Skid: the interrupt fires some instructions after the one that caused the event, so blame lands on the wrong line unless you use precise mode.
concepts.L3: Multiplexing is visible in `perf stat` output as a running percentage; if it is below 100 percent the numbers are extrapolations from a fraction of the run, and for events that occur in bursts the extrapolation can be badly wrong. The remedy is to measure fewer events per run and repeat. Skid is more insidious because the output looks perfectly plausible: a hot line one or two instructions after the real one, which is enough to send you optimising the wrong statement. PEBS on Intel and IBS on AMD have the hardware record the instruction pointer at the event rather than at the interrupt, and `perf record -e cycles:pp` requests it.

L4.explanation: Skid is typically a few instructions but can cross a basic block boundary, which is how it produces obviously impossible attributions. Any time a profile blames something that cannot generate the event, suspect skid before suspecting the compiler.

For measurement, set the governor to `performance` and disable turbo so the clock is a constant; this makes runs comparable at the cost of not representing production. On GPUs the same applies through clock throttle reasons reported by `nvidia-smi`.

L4.prompt_tpl: A part has a base clock of {base} GHz, a single-core turbo of {st} GHz and an all-core turbo of {at} GHz. A benchmark measures {ips} instructions per second on one core. Estimate the per-core rate when all cores are loaded, and the error in extrapolating from the single-core number. Answer with the per-core instruction rate when all cores are loaded.
L4.answer: Scale by the frequency ratio: per-core rate $= ips \cdot at/st$. For $st=4.5$, $at=3.2$: $0.711 \cdot ips$, so about $5.7\times10^{9}$. Extrapolating the single-core number overstates per-core throughput by $st/at - 1 = 41$ percent.
L4.explanation: This assumes frequency is the only difference, which understates the real gap because shared caches, memory bandwidth and coherence traffic all worsen at full load too. Treat the frequency correction as a lower bound on the extrapolation error.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your CI reports a {pct} percent regression that does not reproduce locally. turbostat on the CI machine shows Bzy_MHz varying between runs. What do you change?
options: Increase the iteration count so the noise averages out
Pin the governor to performance and disable turbo on the CI machine, then interleave the two builds
Move the benchmark to a larger CI instance with more cores
L4.answer: Pin the governor to performance and disable turbo on the CI machine, then interleave the two builds
L4.explanation: Frequency variation is a systematic bias, not zero-mean noise, so more iterations do not remove it and can make it worse by heating the part further. Fixing the clock makes the measurement about the code, and interleaving protects against any residual drift.

L0.body:
turbostat --show Core,Bzy_MHz,PkgTmp,PkgWatt --interval 1 -- ./bench
#  PkgTmp climbing toward ~100 C with Bzy_MHz falling = thermal throttle

nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks_throttle_reasons.active \
             --format=csv -l 1        # HW_SLOWDOWN, SW_THERMAL_SLOWDOWN...

# Hygiene checklist for any A/B comparison:
#   1. fixed governor, turbo off      4. interleave A B A B, randomise order
#   2. idle machine, no other tenants 5. discard the first runs (warm-up)
#   3. log temperature every run      6. re-measure BOTH after any rebuild
L0.cloze:
Falling {{c1::Bzy_MHz}} with rising package temperature is the signature of thermal throttling.
On GPUs, check `{{c2::clocks_throttle_reasons.active}}`.
Always {{c3::interleave}} the two arms and log {{c4::temperature}} per run.

concepts.L1: Silicon reduces frequency when it approaches its thermal limit. Because heating is cumulative over a run, throttling introduces a time-dependent bias: later measurements are systematically slower than earlier ones, independent of the code being measured.
concepts.L2: This is why running all of A then all of B is not a design flaw of taste but a source of confident wrong answers. The second arm runs hotter, so it loses; swap the order and it wins. If a result flips when you reverse the order, temperature was your independent variable.
concepts.L3: Treat the machine as an instrument that drifts. The first defence is to remove the drift: an idle machine, a fixed governor, turbo disabled, and adequate cooling headroom, which on a laptop is usually unattainable and on a rack server usually is. The second is to make the experiment insensitive to whatever drift remains: interleave the arms, randomise order within the interleaving, and discard an initial warm-up period so all measured runs share a similar thermal state. The third is to detect it rather than assume it away: log package temperature and busy frequency for every run and plot them against run index.

L4.prompt_tpl: A comparison shows B is {pct} percent slower than A. Re-running with the order reversed shows A is about {pct} percent slower than B. What is the independent variable, and how do you fix the experiment?
L4.answer: Machine state, almost certainly thermal: whichever arm runs second is penalised because the part has heated and dropped frequency. Fix by interleaving A and B run by run, randomising the order, discarding warm-up runs, pinning the governor and disabling turbo, and logging package temperature and busy frequency alongside each measurement so the drift is visible rather than inferred.
L4.explanation: The order-reversal test is the cheapest possible check and should be run before reporting any result from a single ordered block. A result that survives order reversal is at least not thermally confounded.

L4.prompt_tpl: A GPU kernel benchmark reports {tf} TFLOP/s in the first {s} seconds and 20 percent less thereafter, with no code change. Name the two throttle classes and how you would distinguish them.
L4.answer: Power limit and thermal limit. Query clocks_throttle_reasons.active with nvidia-smi: SW_POWER_CAP indicates the board is at its power limit, while SW_THERMAL_SLOWDOWN or HW_THERMAL_SLOWDOWN indicates temperature. Also log power.draw against power.limit and temperature.gpu. The remedies differ: a power limit is a provisioning or clock-cap decision, a thermal limit is a cooling problem.
L4.explanation: Reporting a peak number achieved in the first seconds is a common and misleading practice, since sustained throughput is what a training run experiences. Always quote the steady-state figure and say how long you ran to reach it.

concepts.t: The energy cost of moving a byte

L0.body:
# Approximate energy per operation at 45 nm (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014).
# The ABSOLUTE numbers shrink with process node; the RATIOS barely do.
#   int8 add                 0.03 pJ
#   int32 add                0.1  pJ
#   fp16 add                 0.4  pJ
#   fp32 add                 0.9  pJ
#   fp32 multiply            3.7  pJ
#   8 KB SRAM read, 32 bit   5    pJ      ~ 5x an fp32 add
#   DRAM read, 32 bit        640  pJ      ~ 700x an fp32 add
#
# Therefore: an accelerator is a machine for NOT moving data.
# Tiling, fusion, on-chip SRAM and reduced precision are all the same idea.
L0.cloze:
At 45 nm an fp32 add costs about {{c1::0.9}} pJ while a 32-bit DRAM read costs about {{c2::640}} pJ, roughly {{c3::700}}x.
The absolute numbers shrink with process node but the {{c4::ratios}} do not.
Accelerator design is therefore about not {{c5::moving data}}.

concepts.L1: Arithmetic is nearly free; moving the operands is not. Published energy figures at 45 nm put an fp32 add under a picojoule and a 32-bit DRAM read at several hundred, a ratio of roughly two to three orders of magnitude, with on-chip SRAM sitting in between.
concepts.L2: This inverts the intuition that FLOPs are the resource. If a DRAM access costs what hundreds of adds cost in energy, recomputing a value is often cheaper than storing and reloading it, which is exactly why FlashAttention recomputes in the backward pass instead of saving activations.
concepts.L3: Use the ratios as a design rule, since the absolute picojoule figures are process-specific and the 45 nm table is a reference point rather than a current measurement. Ordering from cheap to expensive: register file, on-chip SRAM, on-package HBM, off-package DRAM, then the interconnect to another chip, each step roughly an order of magnitude. Every efficiency technique in modern accelerators is an application of this ordering. Tiling and blocking keep operands in registers and SRAM. Fusion avoids a round trip to HBM. Reduced precision halves the bytes moved for the same arithmetic. When you evaluate an architectural idea, count the bytes it moves at each level before counting its operations.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using {ea} pJ per fp32 add and {ed} pJ per 32-bit DRAM read, compute the energy of a kernel that performs {f} FLOPs and moves {b} 32-bit words from DRAM, and give the fraction spent on data movement. Answer with the fraction of energy spent on data movement.
L4.answer: compute $= f \cdot ea$; movement $= b \cdot ed$; fraction $= $ movement$/($compute $+$ movement$)$. For $f=10^{8}$, $b=10^{7}$: compute $9\times10^{7}$ pJ, movement $6.4\times10^{9}$ pJ, so 98.6 percent is data movement.
L4.explanation: At an arithmetic intensity of 10 FLOP per word, nearly all the energy is movement. Only at intensities in the hundreds does arithmetic begin to matter, which is the energy analogue of the roofline ridge point and lands in a similar place.

L4.prompt_tpl: FlashAttention recomputes the {n}-by-{n} attention scores in the backward pass rather than storing them. Justify this against the energy and bandwidth costs.
L4.answer: Storing them means writing an $n^{2}$ matrix to HBM in the forward pass and reading it back in the backward pass, which is order $n^{2}$ bytes of the most expensive traffic and also order $n^{2}$ of memory capacity. Recomputing costs order $n^{2}d$ FLOPs on tensor cores that were idle waiting on memory, at an energy per operation two to three orders of magnitude below a DRAM access. The kernel was memory bound, so the extra arithmetic is free in time as well as cheap in energy.
L4.explanation: This is the general shape of the recompute-versus-store trade, and it is why gradient checkpointing works. It only holds while you are below the roofline ridge point; a compute-bound kernel would pay for the recomputation in time.
